Can In-Context Learning Support Intrinsic Curiosity?Thanks: Equal contribution. Correspondence to: {eric.elmoznino,guillaume.lajoie}@gmail.com, sangnie@google.com

Eric Elmoznino    Sangnie Bhardwaj Affiliation: Google – Paradigms of Intelligence Team, Google DeepMind    Johannes von Oswald    Rajai Nasser    Blaise Agüera y Arcas    João Sacramento    Rif A. Saurous    Guillaume Lajoie
Abstract

Effective machine learning depends not only on how we model data, but also on what data we choose to collect. While large sequence models have revolutionized data modeling, the problem of automated data selection, or “intrinsic curiosity”, remains a significant challenge. Classic approaches incentivize exploration by rewarding an agent based on its “learning progress”, which measures how much a newly acquired observation improves a world model’s predictive ability. However, evaluating these rewards traditionally requires expensive inner loops of gradient descent updates within each trajectory, rendering them computationally impractical at scale. In this work, we investigate whether the emergent in-context learning (ICL) capabilities of sequence models can eliminate this bottleneck by serving as immediate, update-free world models. Specifically, we evaluate whether an exploration policy can be trained to maximize learning progress, using solely the prediction errors and counterfactual context manipulations of an in-context learner. We first prove that in general Markov decision processes, this is in fact impossible in an unbiased way: the resulting intrinsic rewards either suffer from nuisance terms that bias their estimation of true learning progress, or they cannot be implemented using an in-context learner’s prediction errors. Conversely, we prove a positive result for a broad subclass of non-temporal settings, encompassing active learning and Bayesian Experimental Design: here, ICL-derived rewards successfully bound and asymptotically converge to the true learning progress. We corroborate our theory with controlled experiments across continuous and symbolic environments, demonstrating that our ICL-driven framework successfully trains curious data-collection policies that explore optimally.

1 Introduction

How should an agent collect data in an unknown environment to ensure optimal exploration? One foundational approach dictates that the data should maximally improve the agent’s model of its environment (Schmidhuber, 1991b; Lindley, 1956). Such a model can subsequently support arbitrary downstream tasks, either through explicit planning or by having acquired robust representations. To this end, prior work has proposed utilizing “intrinsic rewards” to drive the collection of data, which are defined strictly as a function of the trajectory of actions and observations collected by a policy, and assume no extrinsic “task”.

Given a Bayesian prior on the world, an optimal intrinsic reward is Bayesian information gain (BIG), which measures the expected bits gained about the true environment’s dynamics with every action (Itti and Baldi, 2009; Lindley, 1956). However, BIG is difficult to compute in practice because it requires explicitly parameterizing the environment’s dynamics and performing intractable Bayesian inference. While tractable prediction-based objectives have been proposed as alternatives (Schmidhuber, 1991b, e.g.,), they face two major hurdles: (1) their theoretical relationship to BIG remains poorly understood and (2) computing them requires expensive gradient descent updates to a world model that have slow credit assignment.

Overcoming this second bottleneck requires fast and data-efficient learning mechanisms. In-context learning (ICL) has emerged as a highly effective paradigm for addressing this problem: sequence models can act as amortized predictors that implicitly approximate the Bayesian posterior predictive in a single forward pass, bypassing the need for explicit inference. This capability is hypothesized to partly drive the success of large language models (Radford et al., 2019; Brown et al., 2020), and has seen great success with Prior-Fitted Networks (PFNs) (Nagler, 2023; Müller et al., 2022) such as TabPFN (Hollmann et al., 2022) which are pretrained on a large prior over datasets to perform amortized learning on a new dataset at inference time.

In this work, we use ICL for evaluating prediction-based intrinsic curiosity rewards. We examine the degree to which data collected by a policy improves a world model learned purely in-context, and reward the policy based on this improvement. This raises several fundamental questions: First, is this possible with ICL, and for which intrinsic rewards? Second, does the resulting reward approximate BIG, and if so, under what circumstances? To answer these questions, we make the following contributions:

  1. 1.

    By formalizing in-context learners as implicit Bayesian predictors, we prove novel mathematical relationships between prediction-based intrinsic rewards and BIG, which were previously unknown.

  2. 2.

    We provide a negative result for general Markov Decision Processes (MDPs), proving that prediction-based intrinsic rewards are biased estimators of BIG. Further, while some of these rewards can be implemented using ICL, we show that others, such as classic learning progress (Schmidhuber, 1991b), cannot.

  3. 3.

    In contrast, we establish a positive result for Bayesian Experimental Design (BED) settings, demonstrating that several intrinsic rewards can be approximated using ICL, and that it is possible to asymptotically approximate BIG for long trajectories with a particular reward structure.

  4. 4.

    We conduct experiments that corroborate our theoretical findings, demonstrating the practical viability of this ICL approach to curiosity.

2 Problem Setting and Notation

Environment.

We consider a Bayes-Adaptive MDP (BAMDP) with states sts_{t}, actions ata_{t}, horizon TT, and a latent environment parameter θ∼p⁡(θ)\theta\sim p(\theta) fixed throughout an episode. Conditional on θ\theta, the environment’s dynamics are Markov and stationary: st+1∼p(⋅∣st,at,θ)s_{t+1}\sim p(\cdot\mid s_{t},a_{t},\theta). Throughout, we write ht≔(s1,a1,…,st−1,at−1)h_{t}\coloneqq(s_{1},a_{1},\ldots,s_{t-1},a_{t-1}) for the trajectory history just before sts_{t}.

Intrinsic curiosity objective.

Our goal is to train a policy πϕ​(at∣ht,st)\pi_{\phi}(a_{t}\mid h_{t},s_{t}) under a “meta-RL” setting (Duan et al., 2016) in which episodes are rolled out from environments sampled from p⁡(θ)p(\theta). Crucially, there is no notion of “task” or “extrinsic” reward. We instead consider “intrinsic” rewards that are functions of only the trajectory (s1,a1,…,sT)(s_{1},a_{1},\ldots,s_{T}), and which are ideally maximized when the trajectory is highly informative about the latent parameters θ\theta governing the environment’s dynamics. By training πϕ\pi_{\phi} across a broad distribution of environments sampled from p⁡(θ)p(\theta), we aim for it to optimally explore a new environment sampled from this distribution at inference time. In information theoretic terms, we consider an “optimal” intrinsic reward as one that maximizes the per-step mutual information between an observed state and the latent environment parameters, conditioned on the history. In the literature, this is called Bayesian information gain (BIG) or Bayesian surprise (Itti and Baldi, 2009; Lindley, 1956):

BIG:=I⁡(st;θ∣ht).\displaystyle\text{BIG}:=I(s_{t};\theta\mid h_{t}). (1)
In-context learning prediction errors.

We consider whether a sequence model ρ\rho can be used to approximate BIG, using only its prediction errors and manipulations of its context. We assume that ρ\rho has been pretrained offline to perform next-state predictions on trajectories of BAMDPs sampled from prior p⁡(θ)p(\theta) with uniform action selection — ρ\rho is then frozen when training the policy. We further suppose that ρ\rho has been trained with sufficient capacity and data, such that it has learned to emit the Bayesian posterior-predictive:

ρ⁡(st∣ht)=∫p⁡(st∣st−1,at−1,θ)​p​(θ∣ht)​𝑑θ.\displaystyle\rho(s_{t}\mid h_{t})=\int p(s_{t}\mid s_{t-1},a_{t-1},\theta)\,p(\theta\mid h_{t})\,d\theta. (2)

This perspective of in-context learners as amortized Bayes-optimal predictors has been formalized in substantial prior work (Grau-Moya et al., 2024; Mikulik et al., 2020; Xie et al., 2022; Binz et al., 2024; Nagler, 2023; Müller et al., 2022), and it serves as a starting point for our investigations. In our setting, ρ\rho can be seen as a meta-learner that implicitly fits environment parameters θ\theta in-context and exposes their predictions for novel transitions, all within a single forward pass. The speed of in-context learners makes them particularly promising for the purposes of optimizing certain intrinsic curiosity objectives, which, as we will see next, require us to repeatedly assess the learning progress of a world model over the course of a trajectory.

3 Prior Work on Intrinsic Curiosity

We briefly describe approaches to intrinsic curiosity relevant to our work — Aubret et al. (2023) provides a recent review. We discuss intrinsic rewards that are less directly related to our work in Appendix A. We assume p(⋅∣⋅,θ^t)p(\cdot\mid\cdot,{\hat{\theta}_{t}}) is a predictive world model that has been trained on subtrajectory (a1:t−1,s1:t)(a_{1:{t-1}},s_{1:t}).

Surprisal.

A common heuristic for encouraging exploration is to maximize a world model’s surprisal, seeking observations for which it has high prediction error. The surprisal reward is rt≔−log⁡p⁡(st∣st−1,at−1,θ^t−1)r_{t}\coloneqq-\log\ p(s_{t}\mid s_{t-1},a_{t-1},\hat{\theta}_{t-1}). This approach has been used at least as far back as Schmidhuber (1991a) and is simple but surprisingly effective (Burda et al., 2019; Levy et al., 2025; Hester and Stone, 2012; Chentanez et al., 2004). However, surprisal fails to distinguish between two sources of information: epistemic (i.e., learnable) and aleatoric (i.e., noise). The latter can be detrimental: a policy seeking surprisal will learn to sit in front of a “noisy TV”, even if these observations contain no new useful information about the environment (Schmidhuber, 1991b). Thus, while surprisal excels in deterministic environments, it fails in stochastic settings (Burda et al., 2019).

Learning progress.

Another principled approach to intrinsic curiosity is to maximize “learning progress”, introduced in Schmidhuber (1991b) and further explored in (Schmidhuber, 2009; Schmidhuber, 2010; Storck et al., 1995; Oudeyer et al., 2007; Oudeyer and Kaplan, 2008; Oudeyer and Kaplan, 2007; Lopes et al., 2012; Azar et al., 2019). It aims to reward a policy based on the degree to which the data that it acquires improves the predictive ability of a world model. The learning progress intrinsic reward is rt≔log⁡p⁡(st∣st−1,at−1,θ^t)−log⁡p⁡(st∣st−1,at−1,θ^t−1)r_{t}\coloneqq\log\ p(s_{t}\mid s_{t-1},a_{t-1},\hat{\theta}_{t})-\log\ p(s_{t}\mid s_{t-1},a_{t-1},\hat{\theta}_{t-1}), i.e. the improvement in the model’s ability to predict sts_{t} after the transition to it has been observed. pθ^tp_{\hat{\theta}_{t}} is often parameterized using a recurrent neural network updated online with gradient descent. Unlike surprisal, it assigns zero reward to observations that only contain aleatoric noise, since they do not improve the model’s predictive ability.

In Section 4, we will show that while learning progress has desirable exploration properties, the need to evaluate a model’s prediction error on transitions that it has already seen makes it non-implementable using an in-context learner’s prediction errors, for general environments. Azar et al. (2019) introduced an alternative that instead evaluates improvements in prediction error on future transitions (st+K−1,at+K−1,st+K)(s_{t+K-1},a_{t+K-1},s_{t+K}), rather than on the current one. Section 4 will show that this alternative — along with a variant that considers improvements on all future transitions — can be computed using an in-context learner’s prediction errors.

Bayesian information gain.

Alternatively, we can seek data that maximally changes a model’s belief over possible environments — an approach termed Bayesian information gain (BIG) or Bayesian surprise (Sun et al., 2011; Little and Sommer, 2013; Itti and Baldi, 2009; Houthooft et al., 2016; Stadie et al., 2015; MacKay, 1992; Fedorov, 1972; Houlsby et al., 2011; Lindley, 1956). The predictive model now considers a distribution over possible environment dynamics, with initial prior p⁡(θ^)p(\hat{\theta}). Sun et al. (2011) show that the optimal exploration strategy is to maximize the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the prior and posterior over environment parameters after having observed a novel transition: rt≔KL(p(θ^∣ht,st)||p(θ^∣ht))r_{t}\coloneqq KL(p(\hat{\theta}\mid h_{t},s_{t})\;||\;p(\hat{\theta}\mid h_{t})), where p⁡(θ^∣ht,st)∝p⁡(θ^|ht)​p​(st|ht,θ^)p(\hat{\theta}\mid h_{t},s_{t})\propto p(\hat{\theta}|h_{t})p(s_{t}|h_{t},\hat{\theta}). Intuitively, this objective encourages the agent to reduce its uncertainty about the environment dynamics as quickly as possible. Furthermore, if the initial prior p⁡(θ^)p(\hat{\theta}) is equal to the environment’s true prior distribution over latents p⁡(θ)p(\theta), this reward is mathematically equivalent in expectation to I⁡(st;θ∣ht)I(s_{t};\theta\mid h_{t}) from Equation 1.

While optimal in terms of yielding the fastest convergence of p⁡(θ^∣ht,st)p(\hat{\theta}\mid h_{t},s_{t}) towards the true environment dynamics θ\theta, BIG poses significant implementation challenges. It requires a model to do Bayesian inference over a space of possible environments — an operation that is generally intractable and difficult to approximate. Moreover, this approach assumes the model can explicitly parameterize the hypothesis space over θ\theta, which is challenging in rich environments with unknown latent structure. In Section 4, we will take BIG as the theoretically-optimal objective for intrinsic curiosity, and we will evaluate the degree to which more tractable prediction-based rewards computed with in-context learners can approximate it.

4 Computing Intrinsic Rewards Using In-Context Learners

We now ask whether an in-context learner ρ\rho can support intrinsic curiosity rewards that approximate BIG. Section 4.1 writes candidate rewards in ρ\rho’s interface; Section 4.2 shows none can identify BIG in general BAMDPs at any finite horizon, and that the asymptotic limits required to escape this barrier are practically out of reach; Section 4.3 restores tractability under a structural restriction, namely that of Bayesian Experimental Design (BED).

4.1 Predictive Rewards

We retain the BAMDP setup of Section 2 and additionally write ht′∖th_{t^{\prime}\setminus t} for the history ht′h_{t^{\prime}} with sts_{t} replaced by a “mask” token — a counterfactual manipulation of ρ\rho’s context used by learning-progress-style rewards.

We assume: (i) Markovian, stationary dynamics given θ\theta, (ii) ρ\rho is exactly Bayesian over θ\theta, (iii) the masked trajectory ht′∖th_{t^{\prime}\setminus t} removes only sts_{t}’s contribution and ρ\rho remains exactly Bayesian on it, (iv) posterior consistency: p⁡(θ∣ht)→δθ∗p(\theta\mid h_{t})\to\delta_{\theta^{*}} as t→∞t\to\infty, (v) actions are policy-generated; future actions do not update the posterior over θ\theta, (vi) mixing given θ\theta: I(st;st+k∣θ,ht,at:t+k−1)→0I(s_{t};s_{t+k}\mid\theta,h_{t},a_{t:t+k-1})\to 0 as k→∞k\to\infty. Detailed treatments, including the consequences of approximation, masked-input training, and non-mixing dynamics, are in Appendix B.

We want πϕ\pi_{\phi} to collect observations that are maximally informative about the world, and we investigate how to maximize the stepwise Bayesian information gain (BIG) contributed by a new observation sts_{t}: I⁡(st;θ∣ht)I(s_{t};\theta\mid h_{t}). Importantly, we do not allow explicit access or manipulation of θ\theta, and consider intrinsic rewards reviewed in Section 3 that are built off of state prediction errors, expressed in terms of ρ\rho when possible. Our theoretical results apply to a general class of rewards, including the following common ones:

rtsur\displaystyle r^{\mathrm{sur}}_{t} ≔−log⁡ρ⁡(st∣ht),\displaystyle\coloneqq-\log\ \rho(s_{t}\mid h_{t}), (3)
rtdl\displaystyle r^{\mathrm{dl}}_{t} ≔log∫p(st∣st−1,at−1,θ)p(θ∣ht,st)dθ−logρ(st∣ht).\displaystyle\coloneqq\log\int p(s_{t}\mid s_{t-1},a_{t-1},\theta)\,p(\theta\mid h_{t},s_{t})\,d\theta-\log\ \rho(s_{t}\mid h_{t}). (4)

Here, rsurr^{\mathrm{sur}} is classical predictive surprisal. rdlr^{\mathrm{dl}} is a learning progress reward based on description length (dl) reduction (Schmidhuber, 1991b; Schmidhuber, 2009; Schmidhuber, 2010), which asks how much a just-observed transition would improve a model’s predictions if included in its posterior. Adding to this list, we propose a novel reward:

rtsum\displaystyle r^{\mathrm{sum}}_{t} ≔∑t′=t+1T[log⁡ρ⁡(st′∣ht′)−log⁡ρ⁡(st′∣ht′∖t)],\displaystyle\coloneqq\sum_{t^{\prime}=t+1}^{T}\bigl[\log\ \rho(s_{t^{\prime}}\mid h_{t^{\prime}})-\log\ \rho(s_{t^{\prime}}\mid h_{t^{\prime}\setminus t})\bigr], (5)

where TT is the trajectory length. rsumr^{\mathrm{sum}} is one of our core contributions, and experiments show it performs well (Section 5). It telescopes over the remaining trajectory and is an extension of the NDIGO reward of Azar et al. (2019), which measured the difference in predictive log-likelihoods for a single future observation KK steps in the future. We refer the reader to Section C.6 for a treatment of the NDIGO reward. We illustrate our setting in Figure 1, using rsumr^{\mathrm{sum}} as an example.

4.2 Limits on Intrinsic Rewards From In-Context Learners

We first characterize the class of rewards easily implementable with in-context learners ρ\rho:

1Class ℱ\mathcal{F}.

ℱ\mathcal{F} is the class of arbitrary functions of finitely many predictive likelihoods of ρ\rho at conditioning subsets of the actual trajectory:

ℱ={rt=f((ρ(Xi∣Yi))i∈I):Xi observation, Yi⊆trajectory, ∀i∈I, and f:[0,1]|I|→ℝ}.\displaystyle\mathcal{F}\;=\;\Bigl\{r_{t}=f\bigl((\rho(X_{i}\mid Y_{i}))_{i\in I}\bigr):X_{i}\text{ observation, }Y_{i}\subseteq\text{trajectory, }\forall i\in I\,,\text{ and }f:[0,1]^{|I|}\to\mathbb{R}\Bigr\}.

At any finite horizon TT, rsurr^{\mathrm{sur}} and rsumr^{\mathrm{sum}} belong to ℱ\mathcal{F}. rdlr^{\mathrm{dl}} does not: the integral in Equation 4 requires an explicit Bayesian update of ρ\rho’s posterior — outside ρ\rho’s predictive interface in general (see Appendix D). We return to rdlr^{\mathrm{dl}} in Section 4.3, where it does admit a ρ\rho-tractable form for a subclass of environments. Returning to our goal of maximizing BIG, no finite-horizon reward in ℱ\mathcal{F} can be an unbiased estimator:

1Impossibility of BIG identification in ℱ\mathcal{F}.

Let ℳ\mathcal{M} be the class of BAMDPs satisfying (i)–(v) above, whose transition kernels are neither deterministic nor independent across time given θ\theta. Then for every rt∈ℱr_{t}\in\mathcal{F}, there exists M∈ℳM\in\mathcal{M} with 𝔼M​[rt∣ht]≠I⁡(st;θ∣ht)\mathbb{E}^{M}[r_{t}\mid h_{t}]\neq I(s_{t};\theta\mid h_{t}).

The proof (Section C.2) constructs two BAMDPs whose priors share enough leading moments to match 𝔼⁡[rt]\mathbb{E}[r_{t}] for any finite rt∈ℱr_{t}\in\mathcal{F} while their expected BIG differs. We now decompose rsurr^{\mathrm{sur}} and rsumr^{\mathrm{sum}} against I⁡(st;θ∣ht)I(s_{t};\theta\mid h_{t}) to locate the bias.

2Decomposition of rsurr^{\mathrm{sur}}.

Under (i)–(iii),

𝔼⁡[rtsur∣ht]=I⁡(st;θ∣ht)+H⁡(st∣ht,θ)⏟aleatoric entropy.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[r^{\mathrm{sur}}_{t}\mid h_{t}]\;=\;{I(s_{t};\theta\mid h_{t})}\;+\;\underbrace{\Ent(s_{t}\mid h_{t},\theta)}_{\textnormal{aleatoric entropy}}.

H⁡(st∣ht,θ)=H⁡(st∣st−1,at−1,θ)\Ent(s_{t}\mid h_{t},\theta)=\Ent(s_{t}\mid s_{t-1},a_{t-1},\theta) is non-negative and does not vanish as θ\theta becomes identified.

The proof is in Section C.3. Theorem 2 highlights the classic “noisy TV problem”, where an agent seeks sources of unpredictable noise.

3Decomposition of rsumr^{\mathrm{sum}}.

Under (i)–(iii) and (v),

𝔼[rtsum∣ht,at:T−1]=I(st;θ∣ht)+I(st;st+1∣θ,ht,at)⏟one-step “abductive”−I(st;θ∣ht,at:T−1,st+1:T)⏟“residual”.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[r^{\mathrm{sum}}_{t}\mid h_{t},a_{t:T-1}]\;=\;I(s_{t};\theta\mid h_{t})\;+\;\underbrace{I(s_{t};s_{t+1}\mid\theta,h_{t},a_{t})}_{\textnormal{one-step ``abductive''}}\;-\;\underbrace{I(s_{t};\theta\mid h_{t},a_{t:T-1},s_{t+1:T})}_{\textnormal{``residual''}}.

Both terms are non-negative. Under (iv), the residual vanishes as T→∞T\to\infty; the abductive does not.

The proof is in Section C.4. The abductive term captures kernel-mediated coupling between sts_{t} and the next observation st+1s_{t+1} that is not explained by their common dependence on θ\theta. Similarly, a general treatment of rewards involving log-ratios lead to signal/abductive/residual decomposition (Section C.5). Notably, applied to NDIGO, it produces an analogous decomposition whose abductive and residual both fail to vanish.

Beyond ℱ\mathcal{F}: infinite-horizon rewards.

Taking T→∞T\to\infty to drive rsumr^{\mathrm{sum}}’s residual to zero already pushes rsumr^{\mathrm{sum}} outside the finite-horizon class ℱ\mathcal{F} of Theorem 1. Are there infinite-horizon rewards built from ρ\rho’s predictives that recover BIG in general BAMDPs? Consider the generalization of rsumr^{\mathrm{sum}} with a gap parameter KK separating sts_{t} from the predicted block, rtgap(K)≔logρ(st+K:T∣ht,st,at:T−1)−logρ(st+K:T∣ht,at:T−1)r^{\mathrm{gap}}_{t}(K)\coloneqq\log\ \rho(s_{t+K:T}\mid h_{t},s_{t},a_{t:T-1})-\log\ \rho(s_{t+K:T}\mid h_{t},a_{t:T-1}). Under the mixing assumption (vi), rgapr^{\mathrm{gap}} recovers BIG in the iterated limit limK→∞limT→∞\lim_{K\to\infty}\lim_{T\to\infty} (Corollary 6.1), and this double limit is structurally necessary — any log-ratio reward universally identifying BIG must place all weight at infinite gap with blocks of unbounded size (Theorem 7). We use rgapr^{\mathrm{gap}} as an analytical tool only: it is not feasibly tractable using in-context learners (see below; details in Section C.7).

Summary.

The section identified compounding obstructions to building ρ\rho-based estimators of BIG:

  • •

    Interventional rewards — those requiring modifications of ρ\rho’s posterior — lie outside ρ\rho’s standard interface. The canonical example, rdlr^{\mathrm{dl}} (Equation 4), folds the just-observed sts_{t} into the posterior over θ\theta before re-evaluating the kernel at (st−1,at−1)(s_{t-1},a_{t-1}), and is not implementable through ρ\rho in general BAMDPs.

  • •

    Among ρ\rho-implementable rewards in ℱ\mathcal{F}, no finite-horizon estimator identifies BIG (Theorem 1); rsurr^{\mathrm{sur}} and rsumr^{\mathrm{sum}} exemplify the bias structure, the former acquiring an aleatoric “noisy TV” offset (Theorem 2) and the latter a persistent one-step abductive (Theorem 3).

  • •

    Recovery of BIG via a reward related to ℱ\mathcal{F} requires both sequence length T→∞T\to\infty and marginalizing gap K→∞K\to\infty, as exemplified by the theoretical reward rgapr^{\mathrm{gap}} (Corollaries 6.1 and 7). The latter is a substantial obstacle: significant unobserved intermediate states st+1:t+K−1s_{t+1:t+K-1} that ρ\rho must marginalize over are poorly supported in sequence models (Section B.3).

In sum, we argue there is no practical reward easily implementable with an in-context learner ρ\rho that converges to BIG in general BAMDPs. Moreover, rsumr^{\mathrm{sum}} stands as the best ρ\rho-implementable approximation of BIG — scaling naturally with trajectory length but nevertheless retaining an irreducible abductive bias. We now consider BED, in which several of these obstructions vanish.

4.3 Bayesian Experimental Design Setting

We now consider Bayesian Experimental Design (BED) environments, where the transition kernel satisfies p⁡(st∣st−1,at−1,θ)=p⁡(st∣at−1,θ)p(s_{t}\mid s_{t-1},a_{t-1},\theta)=p(s_{t}\mid a_{t-1},\theta) — the effect of action ata_{t} depends on θ\theta but not on the current state. This covers any sequential experiment with trials conditionally independent given θ\theta and the action sequence, such as active learning. Aleatoric biases remain, and rsurr^{\mathrm{sur}}’s decomposition is unchanged (Theorem 2). But, any abductive bias of the form seen in Theorem 3 vanishes structurally, simplifying rsumr^{\mathrm{sum}}:

3.1Decomposition of rsumr^{\mathrm{sum}} in BED.

Under (i)–(v),

𝔼[rtsum∣ht,at:T−1]=I(st;θ∣ht)−I(st;θ∣ht,at:T−1,st+1:T),\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[r^{\mathrm{sum}}_{t}\mid h_{t},a_{t:T-1}]\;=\;I(s_{t};\theta\mid h_{t})\;-\;I(s_{t};\theta\mid h_{t},a_{t:T-1},s_{t+1:T}),

i.e., the abductive of Theorem 3 vanishes structurally. As T→∞T\to\infty, 𝔼⁡[rtsum]→I⁡(st;θ∣ht)\mathbb{E}[r^{\mathrm{sum}}_{t}]\to I(s_{t};\theta\mid h_{t}).

The proof is in Section C.9. Thus rsumr^{\mathrm{sum}} is an asymptotically unbiased BIG estimator in BED. For rdlr^{\mathrm{dl}} in the BED setting, things also improve. The posterior predictive term admits a ρ\rho-predictive form via a counterfactual action commitment that “copies” the current transition (st−1,at−1,st)(s_{t-1},a_{t-1},s_{t}) into ρ\rho’s context:

∫p⁡(st∣st−1,at−1,θ)​p​(θ∣ht,st)​𝑑θ=ρ⁡(st+1=st|ht,st,at=at−1).\int p(s_{t}\mid s_{t-1},a_{t-1},\theta)\,p(\theta\mid h_{t},s_{t})\,d\theta\;=\;\rho\bigl(s_{t+1}=s_{t}\,\big|\,h_{t},s_{t},\,a_{t}=a_{t-1}\bigr). (6)

The counterfactual is the action choice at=at−1a_{t}=a_{t-1} (re-using the same action), valid because actions are policy-generated and the BED environment’s transition kernel has no st−1s_{t-1} dependence. The identity in Equation 6 makes rdlr^{\mathrm{dl}} implementable using in-context learners at the cost of a hypothetical extra rollout step.

4Decomposition of rdlr^{\mathrm{dl}} in BED.

Under (i)–(v), with L⁡(θ)≔p⁡(st∣at−1,θ)/ρ⁡(st∣ht)L(\theta)\coloneqq p(s_{t}\mid a_{t-1},\theta)/\rho(s_{t}\mid h_{t}),

𝔼⁡[rtdl∣ht]=I⁡(st;θ∣ht)+𝔼st|at−1​[log⁡𝔼p⁡(θ∣ht,st)​[L⁡(θ)]−𝔼p⁡(θ∣ht,st)​[log⁡L⁡(θ)]],\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[r^{\mathrm{dl}}_{t}\mid h_{t}]\;=\;I(s_{t};\theta\mid h_{t})\;+\;\mathbb{E}_{s_{t}\mid a_{t-1}}\!\Bigl[\log\ \mathbb{E}_{p(\theta\mid h_{t},s_{t})}[L(\theta)]-\mathbb{E}_{p(\theta\mid h_{t},s_{t})}[\log\ L(\theta)]\Bigr],

i.e., BIG plus a non-negative Jensen gap. Both terms in the expectation vanish as t→∞t\to\infty under (iv).

The proof is in Section C.10. Like rsumr^{\mathrm{sum}}, rdlr^{\mathrm{dl}} converges to BIG in BED, but with opposite-sign bias: rsumr^{\mathrm{sum}} is biased downward by a residual on future data, rdlr^{\mathrm{dl}} upward by a Jensen gap on past data. We thus get 𝔼⁡[rtsum]≤I⁡(st;θ∣ht)≤𝔼⁡[rtdl]\mathbb{E}[r^{\mathrm{sum}}_{t}]\leq I(s_{t};\theta\mid h_{t})\leq\mathbb{E}[r^{\mathrm{dl}}_{t}], with the gap closing asymptotically. Importantly, however, it should be noted that rdlr^{\mathrm{dl}}’s bias (the Jensen gap) vanishes together with BIG I⁡(st;θ∣ht)I(s_{t};\theta\mid h_{t}) itself, as t→∞t\to\infty (see Section C.9).

Summary.

BED removes the obstructions of general BAMDPs: rsumr^{\mathrm{sum}} and rdlr^{\mathrm{dl}} both asymptotically recover BIG. However, rsumr^{\mathrm{sum}} recovers BIG as T→∞T\to\infty while rdlr^{\mathrm{dl}} does so as t→∞t\to\infty. This means that given long sequences, rsumr^{\mathrm{sum}} can, in principle, recover BIG at finite tt while rdlr^{\mathrm{dl}} only trivially recovers BIG in the limit where the signal itself vanishes. Nevertheless, both rewards can still be useful at finite TT and finite tt, as we now investigate in experiments.

5 Experiments

We evaluate our framework on three structured BED environments: Gaussian Process function estimation, Mastermind code-breaking, and Alchemy transition-rule discovery, each requiring the policy to actively gather observations that are informative about unknown latent variables.

We train policies with PPO or REINFORCE using curiosity-driven rewards from Section 4.1: rsurr^{\mathrm{sur}}, rdlr^{\mathrm{dl}}, and rsumr^{\mathrm{sum}}. We also compare to rtaskr^{\mathrm{task}}, which uses a validation metric of the environment (indicative of having learned its dynamics) as the reward. For each environment, we pretrain an in-context learner ρ\rho by sampling environment latents from the prior θ∼p⁡(θ)\theta\sim p(\theta) and unrolling trajectories with uniformly-random actions; as such, we call these Prior-Fitted Networks (PFNs) in line with prior work (Müller et al., 2022). Some environments additionally admit an exact predictive Bayesian oracle predictive ρ∗\rho^{*}. Details and results for each environment are given below.

5.1 Gaussian Process

The Gaussian Process (GP) environment models active function estimation in a continuous domain. An unknown function ff is sampled from a GP prior with a rational quadratic kernel. The function ff is represented by a finite set of inducing points sampled on a regular grid of resolution RR over the domain [−xmax,xmax]2[-x_{\max},x_{\max}]^{2}; the posterior mean at any query location is obtained by exact GP conditioning on these inducing points. More details can be found in Section E.1.1.

A fresh function ff is drawn at the start of each episode. At each step the policy selects a query location xt∈[−xmax,xmax]2x_{t}\in[-x_{\max},x_{\max}]^{2} and observes a noisy evaluation yt=f⁡(xt)+εty_{t}=f(x_{t})+\varepsilon_{t}, where εt∼𝒩⁡(0,σnoise2​(xt))\varepsilon_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}\bigl(0,\,\sigma_{\mathrm{noise}}^{2}(x_{t})\bigr) is spatially varying noise. The noise is in the form of a tiled checkerboard pattern (details in Section E.1.1), and is the same in every episode. An optimal information-gathering policy should therefore learn to preferentially query the low-noise tiles. Consecutive observations are conditionally independent given ff and the noise map. Therefore, the environment follows the BED setting with θ=f\theta=f, at=xta_{t}=x_{t}, and st+1=yts_{t+1}=y_{t}.

Predictive model.

The Bayesian oracle ρ∗\rho^{*} performs exact GP posterior inference. After observing hth_{t}, the predictive distribution for yty_{t} is ρ∗​(yt∣ht,xt)=𝒩⁡(yt,μt​(xt),σt2​(xt))\rho^{*}(y_{t}\mid h_{t},x_{t})=\mathcal{N}\!\bigl(y_{t};\;\mu_{t}(x_{t}),\;\sigma^{2}_{t}(x_{t})\bigr) where μt\mu_{t} and σt2\sigma^{2}_{t} are the standard GP posterior mean and predictive variance (including observation noise) conditioned on hth_{t}. Note ρ∗\rho^{*} has access to the true kernel and the noise map. The learned PFN ρ\rho is a causal Transformer. Details about the training and architecture are in Section E.1.3. We also show in Figure E.1 that ρ\rho approximates ρ∗\rho^{*} well.

Validation.

To measure the quality of the collected trajectory hTh_{T}, we evaluate on a set of validation points on the grid. Let (Xv​a​l,Yv​a​l)={(x~j,y~j)}j=1M(X_{val},Y_{val})=\{(\tilde{x}_{j},\tilde{y}_{j})\}_{j=1}^{M} be a random subset of the episode’s ground-truth GP inducing points. Regardless of whether ρ\rho is a Bayesian oracle or a trained PFN, we validate by conditioning the oracle ρ∗\rho^{*} on the trajectory hTh_{T} and report the mean log-likelihood V=1M​∑j=1Mlog⁡ρ∗​(y~j∣hT,x~j)V=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{j=1}^{M}\log\rho^{*}(\tilde{y}_{j}\mid h_{T},\,\tilde{x}_{j}).

Results.

Since the environment contains aleatoric noise, we observe a stark divergence in performance between the rewards. As shown in Figure 2, both the random baseline and the policy trained with rsurr^{\mathrm{sur}} perform significantly worse than those trained with rdlr^{\mathrm{dl}} and rsumr^{\mathrm{sum}}. We note that the validation log-likelihood steadily decreases over training, despite rsurr^{\mathrm{sur}} increasing (Figure E.2). This provides strong empirical confirmation of Theorem 2, which states that rsurr^{\mathrm{sur}} is susceptible to the “noisy TV” problem, whereas rsumr^{\mathrm{sum}} and rdlr^{\mathrm{dl}} successfully distinguish between reducible epistemic uncertainty and irreducible aleatoric noise.

To further confirm this, in Figure 3, we collect 1000 trajectories with a random policy. We then calculate rsurr^{\mathrm{sur}} and rsumr^{\mathrm{sum}} for these trajectories, and in green highlight the ones in the 90% percentile for each reward. We can observe that the trajectories with the highest rsumr^{\mathrm{sum}} stray away from the noisy checkerboards, whereas those for rsurr^{\mathrm{sur}} concentrate in these regions instead. We also plot the BIG across trajectories collected by the policies trained with the different rewards. As predicted, the BIG of rsurr^{\mathrm{sur}} is much lower than that of other rewards. Finally, in Section E.2, we show empirically that rsumr^{\mathrm{sum}} and rdlr^{\mathrm{dl}} decompose into BIG and a shrinking finite-time nuisance term, as predicted by Corollary 3.1 and Theorem 4.

5.2 Mastermind

Mastermind is a code-breaking game parameterized by a secret code c∈{0,…,C−1}Lc\in\{0,\dots,C{-}1\}^{L} made of coloured pegs, where LL is the code length and CC the number of colours. At each step, the policy submits a guess gtg_{t} and receives feedback (bt,wt)(b_{t},w_{t}), where btb_{t} counts the number of pegs correct in both colour and position, and wtw_{t} counts the total number of pegs correct in colour irrespective of position. The feedback depends only on the current guess and the fixed code. This follows the BED setting with θ=c\theta=c, at=gta_{t}=g_{t}, and st+1=(bt,wt)s_{t+1}=(b_{t},w_{t}).

We additionally consider a noisy variant of the environment in which one randomly chosen colour per episode is designated as “evil.” Any guess position whose colour matches the evil colour has that position’s value replaced with a uniformly random colour before feedback is computed, so the resulting (bt,wt)(b_{t},w_{t}) may not reflect the true code. Additionally, the evil colour is guaranteed not to appear in the secret code itself. The evil colour identity is unknown to the policy and the learned world model ρ\rho.

Predictive model.

The oracle ρ∗\rho^{*} maintains an exact posterior over secret codes by enumerating all CLC^{L} possibilities and filtering to those consistent with the observed history. It computes the predictive probability of each new response as the fraction of consistent codes that would produce that response:

ρ∗(st∣ht)=|{c′:c′​ consistent with ​ht​ and ​(at−1,st)}||{c′:c′​ consistent with ​ht}|.\rho^{*}(s_{t}\mid h_{t})=\frac{|\{c^{\prime}:c^{\prime}\text{ consistent with }h_{t}\text{ and }(a_{t-1},s_{t})\}|}{|\{c^{\prime}:c^{\prime}\text{ consistent with }h_{t}\}|}.

ρ∗\rho^{*} is only tractable when the environment is deterministic. The learned PFN ρ\rho is a causal Transformer pretrained on randomly generated trajectories. More details about consistency, the PFN architecture, and training process are in Sections E.3.1 and E.3.2.

Validation.

After the policy collects a trajectory of TT guesses and responses hTh_{T}, we measure how much probability mass the world model places on the true secret code. We construct a synthetic action/observation pair a~v=c\tilde{a}_{v}=c, s~v=(L,L)\tilde{s}_{v}=(L,L) — the true code paired with a perfect-score response — append it to the trajectory, and report V=ρ∗​(s~v∣hT,a~v)V=\rho^{*}(\tilde{s}_{v}\mid h_{T},\tilde{a}_{v}). For the noisy variant, we use ρ\rho instead of ρ∗\rho^{*}.

Results.

As seen in Figure 4, rsurr^{\mathrm{sur}} achieves near-optimal performance in the standard setup given that the environment has no source of aleatoric noise, matching the performance of training directly for the task. rsumr^{\mathrm{sum}} and rdlr^{\mathrm{dl}} also achieve comparable performance. In this setting, all reward functions perform consistently across both the Bayesian oracle and the trained PFN, further validating that sequence models can serve as effective predictive models for intrinsic reward computation.

However, the introduction of noisy pegs significantly alters these dynamics. In the noisy variant, the performance of the policy trained with rsurr^{\mathrm{sur}} falls even below the random baseline. Conversely, policies trained with rsumr^{\mathrm{sum}} and rdlr^{\mathrm{dl}} remain robust, retaining high performance despite the corruption mechanism. This confirms that rsurr^{\mathrm{sur}} becomes a liability in environments with stochastic transitions, while rsumr^{\mathrm{sum}} and rdlr^{\mathrm{dl}} consistently identify informative actions.

5.3 Alchemy

Alchemy (Wang et al., 2021) is a symbolic meta-learning environment. Each environment defines a fixed set of transition rules mapping (stone, potion) input pairs to transformed output stones, and the agent must discover these rules through sequential experimentation.

The environment is parameterized by a discrete ID θ\theta, which determines the transition dynamics. Stones are four-dimensional discrete vectors whose dimensions have (3,3,3,4)(3,3,3,4) possible values respectively, and potions take one of 6 values. At each step the policy selects both the initial stone and the potion (it,pt)(i_{t},p_{t}) and observes final stone ftf_{t} from the environment. Consecutive observations are conditionally independent given θ\theta (i.e. it+1i_{t+1} is chosen freely and need not equal ftf_{t}). Therefore, Alchemy is BED with at=(it,pt)a_{t}=(i_{t},p_{t}), and st+1=fts_{t+1}=f_{t}.

Similar to Mastermind, we consider a noisy variant of the environment in which one randomly chosen stone type per episode is designated as “evil.” Any transition whose input stone matches the evil stone has its output replaced with a uniformly random stone.

Predictive model.

Like Mastermind, the oracle ρ∗\rho^{*} performs exact Bayesian inference by enumerating all NN candidates, and eliminating those that are not consistent (all observed transitions match θ\theta’s rules). ρ∗\rho^{*} is only tractable when the environment is deterministic. The learned PFN ρ\rho is a causal Transformer with an autoregressive GRU decoder that factorizes output prediction across the components of ftf_{t} (see Section E.4.2 for full architectural and training details).

Validation.

After the policy collects a trajectory of TT transitions hTh_{T}, we evaluate how well the world model can predict held-out transitions from the same environment. From the ground-truth transition table of the current environment ID, we randomly sample M=10M{=}10 transitions, excluding any whose initial stone matches the evil stone (so that only clean transitions are used). These are appended sequentially to the trajectory, and we report the mean predictive log-probability V=1M∑j=1Mlogρ(s~j∣h1:T,a~1:j−1,s~1:j−1)V=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{j=1}^{M}\log\rho(\tilde{s}_{j}\mid h_{1:T},\,\tilde{a}_{1:j-1},\tilde{s}_{1:j-1}). For the non-noisy environment we evaluate under both the Bayesian oracle ρ∗\rho^{*} and the trained PFN ρ\rho; for the noisy (evil stone) variant we evaluate under ρ\rho only.

Results.

We observe a similar pattern as Mastermind in the Alchemy environment in Figure 4. In the noiseless task, rsurr^{\mathrm{sur}} and rsumr^{\mathrm{sum}} both exhibit strong performance, followed by rdlr^{\mathrm{dl}}. Under the noisy variant, rsurr^{\mathrm{sur}} again demonstrates a failure to generalize, with performance below that of a random policy. In contrast, rsumr^{\mathrm{sum}} maintains its superiority with both oracle and PFN, achieving the highest validation log-probability.

The results across all three domains underscore the limitation of surprisal-based curiosity in realistic noisy settings, and demonstrate the robustness of rsumr^{\mathrm{sum}} and rdlr^{\mathrm{dl}}. They also demonstrate the effectiveness of trained in-context learners as predictive models in these settings, as replacements for the intractable BIG.

6 Discussion and Future Work

We demonstrated that in-context learners can efficiently evaluate prediction-based intrinsic curiosity rewards, under certain conditions. In Bayesian Experimental Design (BED) settings, our proposed reward rsumr^{\mathrm{sum}} and description length reward from prior work rdlr^{\mathrm{dl}} asymptotically approximate Bayesian information gain (BIG) and drive exploration effectively, though rdlr^{\mathrm{dl}} suffers from asymptotic pathologies that rsumr^{\mathrm{sum}} avoids. Both avoid the pitfalls of standard surprisal. This framework opens several promising directions for future work.

General BAMDPs.

Extending this approach to general Bayes-Adaptive Markov Decision Processes (BAMDPs) requires handling environments with temporal structure. Implementing rdlr^{\mathrm{dl}} or BIG requires access to a model’s parameters, which is challenging using in-context learners that only expose the model’s predictions. A promising approach is to project the in-context learner’s hidden states into “task vectors” (Hendel et al., 2023) that represent the environment’s latent dynamics. Modulating or manipulating these task vectors counterfactually could allow the direct estimation of rdlr^{\mathrm{dl}} or BIG in latent space. Attempting to approximate rgapr^{\mathrm{gap}} — which asymptotically converges to BIG — using long context lengths and gaps is also a possibility.

Training the in-context learner.

Matching the true Bayesian posterior predictive over the distribution of policy-sampled trajectories during training poses significant challenges. Large foundation models trained on broad data mixtures offer powerful in-context learning, but they are often poorly calibrated to the true Bayesian posterior predictive (Badola et al., 2025). Furthermore, standard causal Transformers suffer from length generalization issues and positional encoding leakage, breaking the martingale properties necessary for Bayesian coherence (Falck et al., 2024). While this is partially mitigated in BED by using permutation-invariant sequence models trained on synthetic priors, covariate shift remains a primary failure mode. Specifically, a model trained on trajectories from a random or fixed policy will degrade when evaluated on informative trajectories collected by an active, reward-maximizing deployment policy (Yadlowsky et al., 2023). Addressing this distribution shift may require techniques that jointly fine-tune the predictive model and the policy (Ross et al., 2011; Ivanova et al., 2024; Azar et al., 2019), though optimizing against non-stationary intrinsic rewards from a changing ρ\rho might introduce instability.

Online RL setting.

This work focuses on an episodic meta-RL setting, but translating these methods to single-lifetime online reinforcement learning introduces several difficulties. First, the fixed context window of sequence models limits the duration over which an agent can accumulate learning progress. Second, in-context learning empirically exhibits saturation; predictive improvements decrease as the context length grows (Elmoznino et al., 2025), perhaps requiring periodic weight updates to consolidate long-term knowledge (Bornschein et al., 2024). Third, the rewards themselves become computationally intractable in continuous online settings. Currently, the intrinsic reward computation is naturally episodic and calculated only at the conclusion of a trajectory (where rsumr^{\mathrm{sum}} evaluates over the remainder of the fully unrolled sequence, and rdlr^{\mathrm{dl}} requires trajectory reruns with the new parameters). Approximating these episodic metrics for online scaling will require stochastic sampling or truncated evaluation windows. Finally, exploration in domains with low-level action spaces is inherently difficult. Leveraging emergent temporal and action abstractions within autoregressive models could allow intrinsic rewards to operate over higher-level behaviors, improving the efficiency of information gathering (Kobayashi et al., 2025).

Comparing rsumr^{\mathrm{sum}} and rdlr^{\mathrm{dl}}.

Empirically, we found that rsumr^{\mathrm{sum}} and rdlr^{\mathrm{dl}} both performed well, but that the optimal one between the two depended on the environment in which they were deployed, suggesting that they can be complementary. Theoretical analysis in BED settings established that rsumr^{\mathrm{sum}} bounds BIG from below, whereas rdlr^{\mathrm{dl}} bounds it from above. The bounds for each are fundamentally different, rdlr^{\mathrm{dl}} converging as t→∞t\to\infty, and rsumr^{\mathrm{sum}} as T→∞T\to\infty. rdlr^{\mathrm{dl}} technically recovers BIG but its bias vanishes together with the signal itself, and rsumr^{\mathrm{sum}} should be more robust and approach BIG at finite tt. However, our experiments show that this distinction may not manifest in simple environments, and at finite TT and tt. Future work might be able to characterize the properties of environments that influence these factors. In addition, because the two bounds converge asymptotically from opposite sides, future work could explore hybridizing them to yield a tighter, more stable estimator of true learning progress.

Appendix A Additional Prior Work on Intrinsic Curiosity

Surprisal in a Learned Latent Space.

One effective approach for mitigating the problem of aleatoric noise is to measure surprisal in a learned latent space that only encodes predictable information about the observation (Pathak et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2019; Burda et al., 2019). However, these methods struggle in partially observed environments where the state representation depends on a long history, and also remain sensitive to sources of aleatoric noise that are produced by the policy’s actions (Burda et al., 2019). Ultimately, the problem of how to train a latent space for surprisal-based exploration that is robust to aleatoric noise remains open. Since our investigation into the use of in-context learners for intrinsic curiosity leverages only ρ\rho’s input/output interface for computing observation-level prediction errors, we do not consider methods that operate in latent space (although if in-context learners are trained in an appropriate latent space, the approach might be viable).

Novelty.

An approach with a long history in reinforcement learning is to seek novel states of the environment, as measured by visitation counts or density models (Hazan et al., 2019; Strehl and Littman, 2008; Bellemare et al., 2016; Ostrovski et al., 2017). Novelty is deeply related to surprisal; while the two are not quite equivalent (Barto et al., 2013), they both suffer from the same fundamental problem: noisy regions of the environment with high observation entropy are a reliable source of both surprisal and novelty.

Empowerment.

Empowerment is an alternative framework for intrinsic motivation that, instead of gathering observations that improve a model of the environment, aims to explore regions of the environment that are controllable by the policy (Klyubin et al., 2005a; Klyubin et al., 2005b; Salge et al., 2014). Specifically, empowerment is defined as the channel capacity of the policy’s actuation channel: I⁡(S′;A∣S)I(S^{\prime};A\mid S) where II is mutual information, SS is a random variable for the history of all past states, AA is a random variable for the agent’s current action, and S′S^{\prime} is a random variable for the state(s) the policy observes after some future horizon following the action (S′S^{\prime} can represent a single future state at a fixed horizon, or potentially a trajectory of such states). The distributions over AA, SS, and S′S^{\prime} depend on both the environment and the policy, and using empowerment as an intrinsic reward involves maximizing I⁡(S′;A∣S)I(S^{\prime};A\mid S) with respect to the latter. Intuitively, this yields policies that learn to exert control over their environment by exploring regions of the state space where actions provide substantial information about future environment dynamics.

It is unclear how empowerment theoretically relates to the above methods that seek to improve a model of the environment. While exploring controllable regions of an environment might improve a model as a side effect (e.g., knowing what is and is not controllable involves understanding the environment’s dynamics at some level), the two are not equivalent in general. While empowerment appears to be a viable exploration strategy empirically (Mohamed and Jimenez Rezende, 2015) and can be highly effective in modeling human exploration behaviour (Du et al., 2023), we instead focus here on intrinsic rewards that explicitly aim to improve a model of the environment.

Open-endedness.

The aims of intrinsic curiosity closely align with those of research on “open-endedness” (Stanley and Lehman, 2015), typically characterized as an ongoing process that continually generates new data, tasks, or behaviours that are interesting, learnable, novel, without being too difficult relative to an agent’s current capabilities. Most existing approaches operationalize open-endedness either through diversity/complexity heuristics (Wang et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2024) or through proxies intended to capture subjective human notions of interestingness (Ding et al., 2023; Bradley et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024).

A recent position paper attempts to mathematically formalize the concept of open-endedness (Hughes et al., 2024), defining it as a process that continually generates data that is (a) surprising and (b) learnable, where both are defined in terms of the prediction errors of a world model that has observed the data up to a particular timepoint. Notably, their learnability component closely resembles learning progress rewards. We further hypothesize that their explicit novelty term is redundant: if learning progress is sustained and does not stagnate, then novelty and surprisal are already implied, because continued progress requires exposure to information not yet captured by the model.

Appendix B Assumptions for Theoretical Results

The main text states six assumptions in compact form. We unpack each here, flagging the nuances that matter for the derivations.

(i) Markovian, stationary dynamics given θ\theta.

For each fixed θ\theta, the transition kernel p⁡(st+1∣st,at,θ)p(s_{t+1}\mid s_{t},a_{t},\theta) is Markov in the state-action chain and time-independent. Stationarity rules out time-indexed families {Pt}t\{P_{t}\}_{t} in which the conditional law itself depends on chain time. Markov dynamics given θ\theta are what let us factorize ρ\rho’s joint over future observations (Lemma 4.1); stationarity ensures that masking-based rewards (rsumr^{\mathrm{sum}} and the NDIGO reward of Azar et al. (2019)) can be evaluated by anchoring their kernels at the actual chain times.

(ii) ρ\rho is exactly Bayesian over θ\theta.

The sequence model emits the exact posterior-predictive ρ⁡(st′∣ht′)=∫p⁡(st′∣st′−1,at′−1,θ)​p​(θ∣ht′)​𝑑θ\rho(s_{t^{\prime}}\mid h_{t^{\prime}})=\int p(s_{t^{\prime}}\mid s_{t^{\prime}-1},a_{t^{\prime}-1},\theta)\,p(\theta\mid h_{t^{\prime}})\,d\theta, with prior p⁡(θ)p(\theta) matching the distribution of training tasks. In practice ρ\rho is a finite-capacity neural network and exact Bayesian computation is an idealization; Section B.2 discusses how approximation error propagates into reward biases.

(iii) Observation-only masking.

The masked history ht′∖th_{t^{\prime}\setminus t} replaces sts_{t} with a mask token while leaving every other state and every action intact. We assume ρ\rho’s response to ht′∖th_{t^{\prime}\setminus t} is the posterior-predictive obtained by Bayesian marginalization over the masked sts_{t}, treating actions as still observed. This is a subtle assumption when ρ\rho is a learned sequence model: masked queries are out-of-distribution unless ρ\rho has been trained to handle them. See Section B.3.

(iv) Posterior consistency.

The selection rule generates trajectories under which p⁡(θ∣ht)→δθ∗p(\theta\mid h_{t})\to\delta_{\theta^{*}} in probability as t→∞t\to\infty. This requires (a) θ\theta identifiability from the achievable observation distributions under the policy and (b) sufficient coverage of the action space (each action taken often enough to inform θ\theta). Under standard regularity conditions (smooth parametric model, positive-definite per-arm Fisher information ℐ⁡(θ)≻0\mathcal{I}(\theta)\succ 0 uniformly on the parameter support), Bernstein–von-Mises gives the rate Var⁡[p⁡(θ∣ht)]∼ℐ​(θ∗)−1/t\mathrm{Var}\!\bigl[p(\theta\mid h_{t})\bigr]\sim\mathcal{I}(\theta^{*})^{-1}/t, controlling both the residual in Theorem 3 and the Jensen gap in Theorem 4 at the 1/t1/t scale. Strictly, the consistency assumption alone is what the framework requires; the Fisher-information regularity becomes relevant only when one wants asymptotic rates rather than asymptotic limits.

(v) Policy-generated actions.

Actions are sampled from πϕ\pi_{\phi} conditional on past observations. Because actions are not generated by the environment, conditioning on a future action does not update the posterior over θ\theta: p⁡(θ∣ht,at,at+1,…,at′−1)=p⁡(θ∣ht)p(\theta\mid h_{t},a_{t},a_{t+1},\ldots,a_{t^{\prime}-1})=p(\theta\mid h_{t}). This permits treating future actions as fixed inputs in the derivations, and is equivalent to the standard interventional treatment of actions in causal Markov chains.

(vi) Mixing given θ\theta.

For each θ\theta in the support of p⁡(θ)p(\theta), I(st;st+k∣θ,ht,at:t+k−1)→0I(s_{t};s_{t+k}\mid\theta,h_{t},a_{t:t+k-1})\to 0 as k→∞k\to\infty. This rules out absorbing states and other non-ergodic dynamics under which the Markov chain never forgets sts_{t}. Mixing is what makes the abductive bias of Theorem 3 (and its rgapr^{\mathrm{gap}}-generalized analogues) decay with the gap parameter KK; without it, infinite-gap rewards still retain a bias from kernel-mediated coupling between sts_{t} and the deep future.

B.1 The Prior p⁡(θ)p(\theta) and Meta-Learning

The prior p⁡(θ)p(\theta) throughout this paper is the training distribution ptrain​(θ)p_{\mathrm{train}}(\theta) over MDPs — ρ\rho is pretrained on trajectories from MDPs sampled from ptrainp_{\mathrm{train}}, and its posterior-predictive is assumed to be Bayesian under ptrainp_{\mathrm{train}}. This is a meta-learning setup, and the framework’s predictions extend to deployment insofar as the deployed environment lies in supp⁡(ptrain)\mathrm{supp}(p_{\mathrm{train}}). We treat deployment mismatch on θ\theta as a separate source of bias and adopt the train-prior framing throughout.

A more pointed meta-learning concern is that ρ\rho’s training data — pairs of trajectories and their corresponding posterior-predictives — depends not only on ptrain​(θ)p_{\mathrm{train}}(\theta) but on the behavior of the policy that generates the training trajectories. Pretraining ρ\rho offline, separately from the deployment policy πϕ\pi_{\phi}, therefore requires the pretraining policy to cover the trajectory distribution adequately. This is mostly tractable in BED settings, where trajectories factorize across actions given θ\theta. Ensuring enough coverage of action selection during training should suffice. It becomes increasingly difficult as the domain expands, and especially in temporally rich BAMDPs where the trajectory distribution depends nonlinearly on the policy: a deployed reward-maximizing policy can easily probe regions that the pretraining policy under-sampled, leaving ρ\rho uncalibrated where it matters most. In principle, this can be alleviated with large enough training samples under enough random policies. Nevertheless, this is a practical matter to be considered.

This is a potential weakness of any offline-pretraining plus online-policy-training scheme: the predictive model is fixed during policy optimization, but policy iteration may drift outside ρ\rho’s effective training support. On the other hand, the scheme opens the door to the use of massive pretrained but frozen foundation models (maybe even LLMs) to support active ICL in a variety of environments. Practical investigations of policy training in this regime, including the robustness of the method to departure from Bayesian exactness of ρ\rho (see next section), and the question of action selection bias, is exciting future work.

Another avenue for the approach to have practical legs at scale would be that of joint training of π\pi and ρ\rho. This could take the form of a meta-learning regime in which the predictor and the data-collection policy improve together so that ρ\rho’s posterior-predictive remains accurate over the trajectories the policy actually generates. We visit this question in Section 6.

B.2 Inexactitude of ρ\rho’s Bayesian Posterior Predictive

Assumption (ii) demands that ρ\rho be exactly Bayesian. In practice ρ\rho is a finite-capacity neural network trained by maximum likelihood on a finite dataset, so it differs from the exact Bayesian posterior-predictive ρ∗\rho^{*} in a controllable but non-zero way. This subsection discusses the consequences of inexactitude as a property of ρ\rho as a learner — independent of any choice about how queries are conditioned on the trajectory. Issues specifically arising from masked queries during training or inference are deferred to Section B.3.

Writing Δ(Y)≔DKL(ρ∗(⋅∣Y)∥ρ(⋅∣Y))\Delta(Y)\coloneqq D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\rho^{*}(\cdot\mid Y)\,\|\,\rho(\cdot\mid Y)) for the per-context KL between exact and approximate predictives at a conditioning YY, each reward inherits a bias that is a signed combination of such KLs. For example,

𝔼ρ∗​[rtsur∣ht]=I⁡(st;θ∣ht)+H⁡(st∣ht,θ)+Δ⁡(ht),\mathbb{E}_{\rho^{*}}[r^{\mathrm{sur}}_{t}\mid h_{t}]\;=\;I(s_{t};\theta\mid h_{t})\;+\;\Ent(s_{t}\mid h_{t},\theta)\;+\;\Delta(h_{t}),

showing that surprisal acquires an additional non-negative Δ⁡(ht)\Delta(h_{t}) on top of the noisy-TV bias. More generally, rewards in ℱ\mathcal{F} formed from log-ratios of predictives at two conditionings Y+,Y−Y_{+},Y_{-} pick up a differential Δ¯​(Y+)−Δ¯​(Y−)\bar{\Delta}(Y_{+})-\bar{\Delta}(Y_{-}) rather than an absolute KL, since the two predictive errors partially cancel under log-subtraction.

Two structural features:

  • •

    rsurr^{\mathrm{sur}}’s bias is absolute. A single non-negative KL Δ⁡(ht)\Delta(h_{t}). Contexts where ρ\rho predicts poorly are systematically over-rewarded, on top of the aleatoric noisy-TV — a model-error-seeking pathology specific to surprisal.

  • •

    Log-ratio rewards have differential bias. Rewards of the form logρ(⋅∣Y+)−logρ(⋅∣Y−)\log\rho(\cdot\mid Y_{+})-\log\rho(\cdot\mid Y_{-}) inherit only the difference of ρ\rho’s errors at Y+Y_{+} and Y−Y_{-}. Uniform approximation error cancels; only the asymmetry between the two conditionings survives.

The differential structure of log-ratio rewards is a robustness property: an across-the-board imperfection in ρ\rho cancels in the log-ratio, leaving only the part of the error that distinguishes the two conditionings. Whether and how this differential is small in practice is a separate question — it depends on how ρ\rho is trained and queried. Figure E.1 in Section E.1.3 shows the difference of log-predictive terms between an oracle observer and a trained PFN ρ\rho for the Gaussian process experiment. Figure 2 in the main text shows very little difference in reward training outcomes for the same experiment.

B.3 Training ρ\rho With vs. Without Masked Inputs

Computing rsumr^{\mathrm{sum}} (and analogously the NDIGO reward of Azar et al. (2019)) requires evaluating ρ\rho on histories with one or more past states masked out. A sequence model trained with standard autoregressive next-token prediction will never have seen a mask token in its training data, so its behavior on masked queries is out-of-distribution. Two training strategies are natural:

Standard autoregressive training.

ρ\rho is trained on natural (unmasked) trajectories. At inference, predictives at masked conditioning sets reflect whatever extrapolation the model performs, with no guarantee of agreement with the Bayesian marginalization over the masked observation. This is the source of the differential bias described in Section B.2.

Masked training.

ρ\rho is trained with random masking of past observations during training, in the spirit of masked language modeling. ρ\rho then learns predictives that are well-calibrated with respect to the marginalized joint, making mask-baseline rewards potentially more reliable.

We remark that these considerations impact reward evaluation in the full BAMDP setting where parts of transition tuples (st−1,at−1,st)(s_{t-1},a_{t-1},s_{t}) need to be masked. However in the BED setting, masking simplifies to simply removing observations from pairs (at−1,st)(a_{t-1},s_{t}) and is not subject to the subtleties described above. Our experiments take place in the BED setting, but a more general implementation of ICL intrinsic rewards should consider the points above.

Appendix C Proofs for Theoretical Results

C.1 Interventional Factorization

Several of our derivations rely on factorizing ρ\rho’s joint over future observations into a product of one-step posterior-predictives. The factorization hinges on two structural features: (a) Markov dynamics given θ\theta (assumption (i)), and (b) policy-generated actions that do not update the θ\theta-posterior (assumption (v)). The second is what makes actions interventional in the causal sense: they enter the joint as fixed inputs, not as random variables to be modeled.

4.1Interventional factorization.

For t1<t2t_{1}<t_{2} and any action sequence at1:t2−1a_{t_{1}:t_{2}-1},

ρ(st1:t2∣ht1,at1:t2−1)=∏τ=t1t2ρ(sτ∣ht1,st1:τ−1,at1:τ−1),\rho(s_{t_{1}:t_{2}}\mid h_{t_{1}},a_{t_{1}:t_{2}-1})\;=\;\prod_{\tau=t_{1}}^{t_{2}}\rho(s_{\tau}\mid h_{t_{1}},s_{t_{1}:\tau-1},a_{t_{1}:\tau-1}),

and the same identity holds with masked histories provided masked states lie outside [t1,t2][t_{1},t_{2}].

Proof.

Under (i), the joint factors as ∏τp⁡(sτ∣sτ−1,aτ−1,θ)\prod_{\tau}p(s_{\tau}\mid s_{\tau-1},a_{\tau-1},\theta). By assumption (v), conditioning on future actions does not update the posterior over θ\theta. Marginalizing θ\theta on both sides gives the product of posterior-predictives. Assumption (iii) extends to masked histories. ∎

This factorization is what allows rsumr^{\mathrm{sum}}’s telescoping representation rtsum=pmi(st;st+1:T∣ht,at:T−1)r^{\mathrm{sum}}_{t}=\pmi(s_{t};s_{t+1:T}\mid h_{t},a_{t:T-1}) to be used in the proof of Theorem 3.

C.2 Proof of Theorem 1

See 1

Remark.

The argument is a marginal-indistinguishability counterexample: we construct two BAMDPs in ℳ\mathcal{M} on which any rt∈ℱr_{t}\in\mathcal{F} has the same unconditional expectation but for which the expected BIG differs. Since an unbiased per-history estimator of BIG forces matched unconditional expectations, the contradiction settles the theorem.

Proof.
Step 1: Unconditional reduction.

Suppose rt∈ℱr_{t}\in\mathcal{F} satisfies the per-history identity 𝔼M​[rt∣ht]=IM​(st;θ∣ht)\mathbb{E}^{M}[r_{t}\mid h_{t}]=I^{M}(s_{t};\theta\mid h_{t}) for every history hth_{t} and every M∈ℳM\in\mathcal{M}. Taking unconditional expectation,

𝔼M​[rt]=𝔼M​[IM​(st;θ∣ht)].\mathbb{E}^{M}[r_{t}]\;=\;\mathbb{E}^{M}\bigl[\,I^{M}(s_{t};\theta\mid h_{t})\,\bigr].

We will exhibit M1,M2∈ℳM_{1},M_{2}\in\mathcal{M} with 𝔼M1​[rt]=𝔼M2​[rt]\mathbb{E}^{M_{1}}[r_{t}]=\mathbb{E}^{M_{2}}[r_{t}] but 𝔼M1​[I⁡(st;θ∣ht)]≠𝔼M2​[I⁡(st;θ∣ht)]\mathbb{E}^{M_{1}}\bigl[I(s_{t};\theta\mid h_{t})\bigr]\neq\mathbb{E}^{M_{2}}\bigl[I(s_{t};\theta\mid h_{t})\bigr], contradicting the per-history identity for at least one of them. We refer to such a pair (M1,M2)(M_{1},M_{2}) — or, since the kernel is fixed in our construction, the corresponding prior pair (p1,p2)(p_{1},p_{2}) — as a witness to the theorem.

Step 2: 𝔼⁡[rt]\mathbb{E}[r_{t}] depends only on the marginal trajectory distribution.

Each rt=f⁡((ρ⁡(Xi∣Yi))i∈I)∈ℱr_{t}=f\bigl((\rho(X_{i}\mid Y_{i}))_{i\in I}\bigr)\in\mathcal{F} has finite touch horizon

Q≔max⁡{τ:τ​ is a chain index appearing in some ​Xi​ or ​Yi},Q\;\coloneqq\;\max\bigl\{\tau:\tau\text{ is a chain index appearing in some }X_{i}\text{ or }Y_{i}\bigr\},

i.e., the largest chain index referenced by the reward. Under Assumption (ii), ρ⁡(X∣Y)=PmargM​(X∣Y)\rho(X\mid Y)=P^{M}_{\mathrm{marg}}(X\mid Y) where PmargMP^{M}_{\mathrm{marg}} is the marginal trajectory law of MM (with θ\theta integrated out). Taking unconditional expectation,

𝔼M​[rt]=𝔼PmargM​[f⁡((PmargM​(Xi∣Yi))i∈I)],\mathbb{E}^{M}[r_{t}]\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{P^{M}_{\mathrm{marg}}}\Bigl[f\bigl((P^{M}_{\mathrm{marg}}(X_{i}\mid Y_{i}))_{i\in I}\bigr)\Bigr],

which depends on MM only through PmargM(s1:Q,a1:Q−1)P^{M}_{\mathrm{marg}}(s_{1:Q},a_{1:Q-1}). In particular, two BAMDPs with identical marginal trajectory distributions on the first QQ steps yield identical 𝔼⁡[rt]\mathbb{E}[r_{t}].

Step 3: A non-degenerate kernel family with prior-dependent BAMDPs.

Take the BAMDP family with state space 𝒮={0,1}\mathcal{S}=\{0,1\}, a single (dummy) action, initial state s1∼Bernoulli⁡(0.5)s_{1}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(0.5), and transition kernel

p⁡(sτ+1≠sτ∣sτ,θ)=θ,θ∈(0,0.5).p(s_{\tau+1}\neq s_{\tau}\mid s_{\tau},\theta)\;=\;\theta,\qquad\theta\in(0,0.5).

The kernel is non-deterministic (θ>0\theta>0) and not independent across time given θ\theta (θ≠0.5\theta\neq 0.5), so each fixed θ∈(0,0.5)\theta\in(0,0.5) yields a kernel meeting the non-degeneracy condition of Theorem 1. Different priors p⁡(θ)p(\theta) supported on (0,0.5)(0,0.5) specify different BAMDPs in ℳ\mathcal{M}.

The marginal trajectory distribution of a sequence s1:Qs_{1:Q} depends only on the number of state flips k=#⁡{τ:sτ+1≠sτ}k=\#\{\tau:s_{\tau+1}\neq s_{\tau}\}:

Pmargp(s1:Q)=12∫00.5θk(1−θ)Q−1−kp(θ)dθ.P_{\mathrm{marg}}^{p}(s_{1:Q})\;=\;\tfrac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{0.5}\theta^{k}(1-\theta)^{Q-1-k}\,p(\theta)\,d\theta.

The integrand is a polynomial in θ\theta of degree at most Q−1Q-1. Expanding,

Pmargp(s1:Q)=12∑j=0Q−1βj(k)mj(p),P_{\mathrm{marg}}^{p}(s_{1:Q})\;=\;\tfrac{1}{2}\sum_{j=0}^{Q-1}\beta_{j}(k)\,m_{j}(p),

where mj​(p)=∫θj​p​(θ)​𝑑θm_{j}(p)=\int\theta^{j}p(\theta)\,d\theta is the jj-th moment of pp and the βj​(k)\beta_{j}(k) are combinatorial constants. Hence Pmargp(s1:Q)P_{\mathrm{marg}}^{p}(s_{1:Q}) depends on pp only through its first Q−1Q-1 moments.

By the truncated Hausdorff moment problem (Schmüdgen, 2017), the set of probability measures on (0,0.5)(0,0.5) matching any prescribed first Q−1Q-1 moments is convex with multiple distinct extreme points. Choose two distinct priors p1,p2p_{1},p_{2} on (0,0.5)(0,0.5) that match in their first Q−1Q-1 moments. Setting M1=(kernel,p1)M_{1}=(\text{kernel},p_{1}) and M2=(kernel,p2)M_{2}=(\text{kernel},p_{2}), both lie in ℳ\mathcal{M}, and by Step 2,

𝔼M1​[rt]=𝔼M2​[rt].\mathbb{E}^{M_{1}}[r_{t}]\;=\;\mathbb{E}^{M_{2}}[r_{t}].
Step 4: Expected BIG differs.

Decompose

𝔼M​[I⁡(st;θ∣ht)]=HmargM​(st∣ht)−𝔼p​[H⁡(st∣st−1,θ)].\mathbb{E}^{M}\bigl[I(s_{t};\theta\mid h_{t})\bigr]\;=\;\Ent^{M}_{\mathrm{marg}}(s_{t}\mid h_{t})\;-\;\mathbb{E}_{p}\bigl[\Ent(s_{t}\mid s_{t-1},\theta)\bigr].

The marginal entropy HmargM⁡(st∣ht)\Ent^{M}_{\mathrm{marg}}(s_{t}\mid h_{t}) is identical for M1M_{1} and M2M_{2} (Step 3, marginals match). The aleatoric term is

𝔼p​[H⁡(st∣st−1,θ)]=𝔼p​[Hbin⁡(θ)],\mathbb{E}_{p}\bigl[\Ent(s_{t}\mid s_{t-1},\theta)\bigr]\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{p}\bigl[\Ent_{\mathrm{bin}}(\theta)\bigr],

where Hbin⁡(θ)=−θ​log⁡θ−(1−θ)​log⁡(1−θ)\Ent_{\mathrm{bin}}(\theta)=-\theta\log\theta-(1-\theta)\log(1-\theta) is the binary entropy function. Since Hbin\Ent_{\mathrm{bin}} is not a polynomial, its expectation under pp is not determined by any finite number of moments of pp. By the truncated moment problem, we may choose p1,p2p_{1},p_{2} matching in the first Q−1Q-1 moments but with 𝔼p1​[Hbin⁡(θ)]≠𝔼p2​[Hbin⁡(θ)]\mathbb{E}_{p_{1}}[\Ent_{\mathrm{bin}}(\theta)]\neq\mathbb{E}_{p_{2}}[\Ent_{\mathrm{bin}}(\theta)]. Therefore 𝔼M1​[I⁡(st;θ∣ht)]≠𝔼M2​[I⁡(st;θ∣ht)]\mathbb{E}^{M_{1}}\bigl[I(s_{t};\theta\mid h_{t})\bigr]\neq\mathbb{E}^{M_{2}}\bigl[I(s_{t};\theta\mid h_{t})\bigr].

Conclusion.

We have 𝔼M1​[rt]=𝔼M2​[rt]\mathbb{E}^{M_{1}}[r_{t}]=\mathbb{E}^{M_{2}}[r_{t}] but 𝔼M1​[I⁡(st;θ∣ht)]≠𝔼M2​[I⁡(st;θ∣ht)]\mathbb{E}^{M_{1}}\bigl[I(s_{t};\theta\mid h_{t})\bigr]\neq\mathbb{E}^{M_{2}}\bigl[I(s_{t};\theta\mid h_{t})\bigr]. The per-history identity 𝔼M​[rt∣ht]=IM​(st;θ∣ht)\mathbb{E}^{M}[r_{t}\mid h_{t}]=I^{M}(s_{t};\theta\mid h_{t}) implies matched unconditional expectations, so it must fail on at least one of M1,M2M_{1},M_{2}. Since the construction works for any rt∈ℱr_{t}\in\mathcal{F}, the theorem follows. ∎
