C.5 The Log-Ratio Subclass and Its Chain-Rule Decomposition

The proof of Theorem 1 settles the impossibility for the entire class ℱ\mathcal{F} via the unconditional reduction. A complementary structural perspective is available for a specific sub-class of ℱ\mathcal{F} — log-ratio rewards — whose expected value reduces to an observation-space mutual information rather than to an entropy. This subsection isolates that sub-class and gives the chain-rule decomposition that underlies the named confound terms in rsumr^{\mathrm{sum}}’s decomposition (Theorem 3) and in the rone​(K)r^{\mathrm{one}}(K) decomposition (Section C.6).

The log-ratio subclass ℱLR\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{LR}}.

For any linear combination of log likelihoods rt=∑ici​log⁡ρ⁡(Xi∣Yi)∈ℱr_{t}=\sum_{i}c_{i}\log\rho(X_{i}\mid Y_{i})\in\mathcal{F}, taking expectation under ρ∗\rho^{*} gives

𝔼[rt]=−∑iciH(Xi∣Yi)=−∑iciH(Xi)+∑iciI(Xi;Yi).\mathbb{E}[r_{t}]\;=\;-\sum_{i}c_{i}\Ent(X_{i}\mid Y_{i})\;=\;-\sum_{i}c_{i}\Ent(X_{i})\;+\;\sum_{i}c_{i}\,I(X_{i};Y_{i}).

The marginal-entropy contribution ∑ici​H⁡(Xi)\sum_{i}c_{i}\Ent(X_{i}) vanishes identically iff, for each distinct random variable XX appearing among the XiX_{i}’s, the coefficients on terms with that XX sum to zero. Rewards meeting this constraint can be written as a sum of matched log-ratios

rt=∑kαk​[log⁡ρ⁡(Xk∣Yk+)−log⁡ρ⁡(Xk∣Yk−)].r_{t}\;=\;\sum_{k}\alpha_{k}\bigl[\log\rho(X_{k}\mid Y_{k}^{+})-\log\rho(X_{k}\mid Y_{k}^{-})\bigr].

We denote this sub-class ℱLR\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{LR}}. Membership:

  • •

    rtsum∈ℱLRr^{\mathrm{sum}}_{t}\in\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{LR}}: each summand is a paired log-ratio with Xk=st′X_{k}=s_{t^{\prime}} for the same future state.

  • •

    rtone​(K)∈ℱLRr^{\mathrm{one}}_{t}(K)\in\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{LR}}: a single paired log-ratio with X=st+KX=s_{t+K}.

  • •

    rtsur∉ℱLRr^{\mathrm{sur}}_{t}\notin\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{LR}}: its single unpaired term −log⁡ρ⁡(st∣ht)-\log\rho(s_{t}\mid h_{t}) has expectation equal to the conditional entropy H⁡(st∣ht)\Ent(s_{t}\mid h_{t}), with the marginal entropy of sts_{t} surviving.

Chain-rule decomposition.

For rt∈ℱLRr_{t}\in\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{LR}}, the expected reward reduces to a signed sum of observation-space conditional MIs:

𝔼⁡[rt]=∑jαj​I​(Aj;Bj∣Cj),\mathbb{E}[r_{t}]\;=\;\sum_{j}\alpha_{j}\,I(A_{j};B_{j}\mid C_{j}),

with Aj,Bj,CjA_{j},B_{j},C_{j} subsets of the trajectory and θ\theta absent from all arguments (since ρ\rho marginalizes over it). Each term decomposes via the chain rule against θ\theta:

I⁡(Aj;Bj∣Cj)=I⁡(Aj;θ∣Cj)⏟signal-like−I(Aj;θ∣Cj,Bj)⏟residual+I(Aj;Bj∣θ,Cj)⏟abductive.I(A_{j};B_{j}\mid C_{j})\;=\;\underbrace{I(A_{j};\theta\mid C_{j})}_{\textnormal{signal-like}}\;-\;\underbrace{I(A_{j};\theta\mid C_{j},B_{j})}_{\textnormal{residual}}\;+\;\underbrace{I(A_{j};B_{j}\mid\theta,C_{j})}_{\textnormal{abductive}}.
Reading the three terms.
  • •

    Signal-like terms quantify how the observation subsets AjA_{j} inform θ\theta given the conditioning CjC_{j}.

  • •

    Residual terms measure the θ\theta-information that AjA_{j} retains after BjB_{j} is also observed.

  • •

    Abductive terms capture dependencies between observation subsets that operate through the kernel’s dynamics rather than through their shared dependence on θ\theta.

This decomposition is exactly what produces the named offsets in Theorem 3 (one-step abductive and residual for rsumr^{\mathrm{sum}}) and in Theorem 5 (KK-step abductive and residual for rone​(K)r^{\mathrm{one}}(K)). It does not extend to rewards outside ℱLR\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{LR}}: rsurr^{\mathrm{sur}} in particular requires its own analysis via the entropy chain rule H⁡(st∣ht)=H⁡(st∣ht,θ)+I⁡(st;θ∣ht)\Ent(s_{t}\mid h_{t})=\Ent(s_{t}\mid h_{t},\theta)+I(s_{t};\theta\mid h_{t}), yielding the BIG-plus-aleatoric form of Theorem 2.

Relation to Theorem 1.

For log-ratio rewards, the chain-rule decomposition gives a useful diagnostic of where the bias relative to BIG comes from: typically a non-vanishing abductive or a non-vanishing residual. It is not, however, the engine of Theorem 1. The proof above (Section C.2) operates at the level of unconditional expectations and works for the entire class ℱ\mathcal{F} uniformly, including non-log-ratio rewards, without invoking the chain-rule decomposition.

C.6 NDIGO reward Decomposition

The NDIGO reward of Azar et al. (2019) is the single-summand analogue of rsumr^{\mathrm{sum}} at horizon KK. We thus refer to it as rone​(K)r^{\mathrm{one}}(K), and define in the ρ\rho setting as:

rtone(K)≔logρ(st+K∣ht,st,at:t+K−1)−logρ(st+K∣ht,at:t+K−1).r^{\mathrm{one}}_{t}(K)\;\coloneqq\;\log\rho(s_{t+K}\mid h_{t},s_{t},a_{t:t+K-1})-\log\rho(s_{t+K}\mid h_{t},a_{t:t+K-1}).
5Decomposition of rone​(K)r^{\mathrm{one}}(K).

Under assumptions (i)–(iii) and (v),

𝔼[rtone(K)∣ht,at:t+K−1]=\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[r^{\mathrm{one}}_{t}(K)\mid h_{t},a_{t:t+K-1}]\;=\;\; I⁡(st;θ∣ht)\displaystyle I(s_{t};\theta\mid h_{t})
+\displaystyle+\; I(st;st+K∣θ,ht,at:t+K−1)\displaystyle I(s_{t};s_{t+K}\mid\theta,h_{t},a_{t:t+K-1})
−\displaystyle-\; I(st;θ∣ht,at:t+K−1,st+K).\displaystyle I(s_{t};\theta\mid h_{t},a_{t:t+K-1},s_{t+K}).
Proof.

By assumption (v), ρ(st∣ht,at:t+K−1)=ρ(st∣ht)\rho(s_{t}\mid h_{t},a_{t:t+K-1})=\rho(s_{t}\mid h_{t}), hence rtone(K)=pmi(st;st+K∣ht,at:t+K−1)r^{\mathrm{one}}_{t}(K)=\pmi(s_{t};s_{t+K}\mid h_{t},a_{t:t+K-1}) (where pmi\pmi is point-wise mutual information). Take expectation and apply the chain rule against θ\theta as in the proof of Theorem 3. ∎

At finite KK the residual I(st;θ∣ht,at:t+K−1,st+K)I(s_{t};\theta\mid h_{t},a_{t:t+K-1},s_{t+K}) does not vanish: a single KK-step-ahead observation does not identify θ\theta. rone​(K)r^{\mathrm{one}}(K) is therefore doubly biased relative to I⁡(st;θ∣ht)I(s_{t};\theta\mid h_{t}) at finite KK (abductive plus persistent residual), and under BED structure reduces to I⁡(st;θ∣ht)I(s_{t};\theta\mid h_{t}) minus a residual. In the limit K→T−tK\to T-t, rone​(K)r^{\mathrm{one}}(K) approaches a single-summand analogue of rsumr^{\mathrm{sum}}.

C.7 Beyond Finite Touch Horizon: The Gap Reward

The decomposition theorems above place rsumr^{\mathrm{sum}} and rone​(K)r^{\mathrm{one}}(K) at opposite structural extremes within the log-ratio subclass:

  • •

    rtsumr^{\mathrm{sum}}_{t} queries the entire future block st+1:Ts_{t+1:T} with no gap. Its epistemic residual vanishes as T→∞T\to\infty (the block contains infinite data, identifying θ\theta), but its one-step abductive I(st;st+1∣θ,ht,at)I(s_{t};s_{t+1}\mid\theta,h_{t},a_{t}) persists — the block starts immediately at t+1t+1, fully coupled to sts_{t} through the Markov kernel.

  • •

    rtone​(K)r^{\mathrm{one}}_{t}(K) queries a single state st+Ks_{t+K} at gap KK. For K→∞K\to\infty in a mixing chain, the abductive I(st;st+K∣θ,ht,at:t+K−1)I(s_{t};s_{t+K}\mid\theta,h_{t},a_{t:t+K-1}) vanishes; but the epistemic residual I(st;θ∣ht,at:t+K−1,st+K)I(s_{t};\theta\mid h_{t},a_{t:t+K-1},s_{t+K}) persists — a single state cannot identify θ\theta.

rsumr^{\mathrm{sum}} controls the residual; roner^{\mathrm{one}} controls the abductive. Each pushes one of two independent structural dials. This invites a unification: query a block that simultaneously starts at a gap KK and extends to the trajectory horizon TT.

2Gap reward.

For 1≤K≤T−t1\leq K\leq T-t,

rtgap(K)≔logρ(st+K:T∣ht,st,at:T−1)−logρ(st+K:T∣ht,at:T−1).r^{\mathrm{gap}}_{t}(K)\;\coloneqq\;\log\rho\bigl(s_{t+K:T}\mid h_{t},s_{t},a_{t:T-1}\bigr)-\log\rho\bigl(s_{t+K:T}\mid h_{t},a_{t:T-1}\bigr).

The two limits of Definition 2 recover the rewards above. At K=1K=1, the conditioning block extends from t+1t+1 to TT and Lemma 4.1 together with assumption (iii) yields rtgap​(1)=rtsumr^{\mathrm{gap}}_{t}(1)=r^{\mathrm{sum}}_{t} exactly. Restricting the block of rtgap​(K)r^{\mathrm{gap}}_{t}(K) to its first state st+Ks_{t+K} recovers rtone​(K)r^{\mathrm{one}}_{t}(K). rgapr^{\mathrm{gap}} is the two-parameter family that interpolates between them by independently choosing a gap KK and a block size T−t−K+1T-t-K+1.

Beyond assumptions (i)–(v), the gap-reward analysis crucially uses assumption (vi): mixing of the chain given θ\theta, ruling out absorbing states and other non-ergodic dynamics under which the chain never forgets sts_{t}.

6Decomposition of rgapr^{\mathrm{gap}}.

Under (i)–(iii) and (v),

𝔼[rtgap(K)∣ht,at:T−1]=\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[r^{\mathrm{gap}}_{t}(K)\mid h_{t},a_{t:T-1}]\;=\;\; I⁡(st;θ∣ht)\displaystyle I(s_{t};\theta\mid h_{t})
+\displaystyle+\; I(st;st+K:T∣θ,ht,at:T−1)⏟abductive at gap ​K\displaystyle\underbrace{I(s_{t};s_{t+K:T}\mid\theta,h_{t},a_{t:T-1})}_{\textnormal{abductive at gap }K}
−\displaystyle-\; I(st;θ∣ht,at:T−1,st+K:T)⏟residual at block end ​T.\displaystyle\underbrace{I(s_{t};\theta\mid h_{t},a_{t:T-1},s_{t+K:T})}_{\textnormal{residual at block end }T}.

Both correction terms are non-negative.

Proof.

By Lemma 4.1, rtgap(K)=pmi(st;st+K:T∣ht,at:T−1)r^{\mathrm{gap}}_{t}(K)=\pmi(s_{t};s_{t+K:T}\mid h_{t},a_{t:T-1}); by (v), ρ(st∣ht,at:T−1)=ρ(st∣ht)\rho(s_{t}\mid h_{t},a_{t:T-1})=\rho(s_{t}\mid h_{t}). Take expectation and apply the chain rule against θ\theta as in the proof of Theorem 3:

I(st;st+K:T∣ht,at:T−1)=\displaystyle I(s_{t};s_{t+K:T}\mid h_{t},a_{t:T-1})\;=\; I(st;θ∣ht,at:T−1)\displaystyle\;I(s_{t};\theta\mid h_{t},a_{t:T-1})
−\displaystyle-\; I(st;θ∣ht,at:T−1,st+K:T)\displaystyle\;I(s_{t};\theta\mid h_{t},a_{t:T-1},s_{t+K:T})
+\displaystyle+\; I(st;st+K:T∣θ,ht,at:T−1).\displaystyle\;I(s_{t};s_{t+K:T}\mid\theta,h_{t},a_{t:T-1}).

By (v), I(st;θ∣ht,at:T−1)=I(st;θ∣ht)I(s_{t};\theta\mid h_{t},a_{t:T-1})=I(s_{t};\theta\mid h_{t}). ∎

Theorem 6 subsumes Theorem 3 (K=1K=1) and reveals that the abductive of rgapr^{\mathrm{gap}} is a KK-shifted analogue of the one-step abductive of rsumr^{\mathrm{sum}}. The decomposition immediately yields a positive counterpart to the impossibility theorem in the iterated infinite limit.

6.1rgapr^{\mathrm{gap}} recovers BIG in the double limit.

Under (i)–(vi),

limK→∞limT→∞𝔼[rtgap(K)∣ht,at:T−1]=I(st;θ∣ht).\lim_{K\to\infty}\;\lim_{T\to\infty}\;\mathbb{E}[r^{\mathrm{gap}}_{t}(K)\mid h_{t},a_{t:T-1}]\;=\;I(s_{t};\theta\mid h_{t}).
Proof.

Inner limit (T→∞T\to\infty, KK fixed). As T→∞T\to\infty the conditioning block st+K:Ts_{t+K:T} grows without bound. Under (iv), p(θ∣ht,at:T−1,st+K:T)→δθ∗p(\theta\mid h_{t},a_{t:T-1},s_{t+K:T})\to\delta_{\theta^{*}} in probability, so the residual I(st;θ∣ht,at:T−1,st+K:T)→0I(s_{t};\theta\mid h_{t},a_{t:T-1},s_{t+K:T})\to 0.

Outer limit (K→∞K\to\infty). With the residual at zero, only the abductive remains. By (i), the dependence of st+K:Ts_{t+K:T} on sts_{t} given θ\theta funnels through st+Ks_{t+K}: I(st;st+K:T∣θ,ht,at:T−1)=I(st;st+K∣θ,ht,at:t+K−1)I(s_{t};s_{t+K:T}\mid\theta,h_{t},a_{t:T-1})=I(s_{t};s_{t+K}\mid\theta,h_{t},a_{t:t+K-1}) (data-processing along the post-st+Ks_{t+K} chain). By (vi), this vanishes as K→∞K\to\infty. ∎

Remarks.
  • •

    Outside ℱ\mathcal{F}. The limit reward in Corollary 6.1 cannot be expressed as a function of finitely many likelihoods, hence not a member of ℱ\mathcal{F}. This is consistent with Theorem 1: at every finite T,KT,K, rtgap​(K)∈ℱLR⊂ℱr^{\mathrm{gap}}_{t}(K)\in\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{LR}}\subset\mathcal{F} and inherits the bias of Theorem 6; only the asymptotic limit escapes ℱ\mathcal{F}.

  • •

    Marginalization burden. Computing rtgap​(K)r^{\mathrm{gap}}_{t}(K) requires ρ\rho to evaluate predictives on histories where sts_{t} is masked and the intermediate states st+1:t+K−1s_{t+1:t+K-1} are absent — effectively asking ρ\rho to marginalize over a gap of K−1K-1 unobserved states. Assumption (iii) — that ρ\rho’s response to such queries is the correctly marginalized posterior-predictive — becomes increasingly strained as the gap grows; see Section B.3.

  • •

    Mixing failure. Assumption (vi) fails for environments with absorbing states or other non-ergodic structure given θ\theta. In such cases the abductive does not decay with KK and the double limit need not yield BIG.

C.8 Necessity boundlessly growing gaps for Log-Ratio Rewards

Corollary 6.1 shows that an infinite gap together with an infinite block is sufficient to recover BIG within a log-ratio reward. We now prove the converse: the same double-limit geometry is also necessary. Concretely, any countable linear combination of matched log-ratios that universally identifies BIG must place all of its weight at infinite gap, with each non-trivial block of infinite size.

Let ℱLR,T\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{LR},T} (cf. Section C.5) be the set of estimators which are linear combinations of log ratios involving subsets of observations up to a horizon TT, i.e.,

ℱLR,T={∑Z⊆{t+1,…,T}cZ[logρ(sZ∣ht,st,at:T)−logρ(sZ∣ht,at:T)]:cZ∈ℝ,∀Z⊆{t+1,…,T}}.\displaystyle\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{LR},T}=\left\{\sum_{Z\subseteq\{t+1,\ldots,T\}}c_{Z}\Bigl[\log\rho(s_{Z}\mid h_{t},s_{t},a_{t:T})-\log\rho(s_{Z}\mid h_{t},a_{t:T})\Bigr]:c_{Z}\in\mathbb{R}\,,\forall Z\subseteq\{t+1,\ldots,T\}\right\}\,.

The following theorem shows that for any sequence of estimators chosen from ℱLR,T\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{LR},T} which is asymptotically equal to the Bayesian Information Gain I⁡(st;θ|ht)I(s_{t};\theta|h_{t}) as T→∞T\to\infty in a universal fashion over all BAMDPs, this sequence must involve an unboundedly growing gap akin to the one discussed in Corollary 6.1.

7Necessity of a growing gap.

Let ℳ\mathcal{M} be the class of BAMDPs satisfying (i)–(vi) whose transition kernels are non-deterministic and not independent across time given θ\theta. Suppose that (Rt,T)T(R_{t,T})_{T} is a sequence of estimators such that

  • •

    Rt,T∈ℱLR,TR_{t,T}\in\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{LR},T} for all TT, i.e.,

    Rt,T=∑Z⊆{t+1,…,T}cZ,T[logρ(sZ∣ht,st,at:T)−logρ(sZ∣ht,at:T)],R_{t,T}=\sum_{Z\subseteq\{t+1,\ldots,T\}}c_{Z,T}\Bigl[\log\rho(s_{Z}\mid h_{t},s_{t},a_{t:T})-\log\rho(s_{Z}\mid h_{t},a_{t:T})\Bigr]\,,
  • •

    limT→∞𝔼M[Rt,T∣ht,at:T]=I(st;θ∣ht)\lim_{T\to\infty}\mathbb{E}^{M}[R_{t,T}\mid h_{t},a_{t:T}]=I(s_{t};\theta\mid h_{t}) for every M∈ℳM\in\mathcal{M} and every ht,at:∞h_{t},a_{t:\infty}, and

  • •

    there exist constants C>0C>0 and B≥1B\geq 1 such that |Wk,T|≤∑kZ=k|cZ,T|≤C​Bk|W_{k,T}|\leq\sum_{k_{Z}=k}|c_{Z,T}|\leq CB^{k} for all kk and TT.11 1 It is worth noting that this is a mild assumption. In practice, numerically stable estimators must satisfy this.

If we define for each block of observations Z⊂{t+1,…}Z\subset\{t+1,\ldots\} the gap kZ≔min⁡{k≥1:t+k∈Z}k_{Z}\coloneqq\min\{k\geq 1:t+k\in Z\} and write

Wk,T≔∑Z⊆{t+1​…,T}:kZ=kcZ,T,W_{k,T}\coloneqq\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}Z\subseteq\{t+1\,\ldots,T\}:\\ k_{Z}=k\end{subarray}}c_{Z,T}\,,

then

limT→∞Wk,T=0.\lim_{T\to\infty}W_{k,T}=0\,.

In other words, as T→∞T\to\infty, almost all the weight ∑ZcZ,T\sum_{Z}c_{Z,T} “will become concentrated on blocks of infinite gap”.

Proof.

Step 1: Chain-Rule Decomposition.
By definition, each matched log-ratio term in ℱLR,T\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{LR},T} evaluates to a pointwise mutual information. Taking the expectation of Rt,TR_{t,T} and applying the chain rule against the environment parameter θ\theta, we obtain:

𝔼M[Rt,T∣ht,at:T]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}^{M}[R_{t,T}\mid h_{t},a_{t:T}] =∑ZcZ,TI(st;sZ∣ht,at:T)\displaystyle=\sum_{Z}c_{Z,T}I(s_{t};s_{Z}\mid h_{t},a_{t:T})
=(∑ZcZ,T)​I​(st;θ∣ht)+∑ZcZ,T​AZ−∑ZcZ,T​EZ,\displaystyle=\Big(\sum_{Z}c_{Z,T}\Big)I(s_{t};\theta\mid h_{t})+\sum_{Z}c_{Z,T}A_{Z}-\sum_{Z}c_{Z,T}E_{Z}\,,

where AZ≔I(st;sZ∣θ,ht,at:T)A_{Z}\coloneqq I(s_{t};s_{Z}\mid\theta,h_{t},a_{t:T}) is the abductive term and EZ≔I(st;θ∣ht,at:T,sZ)E_{Z}\coloneqq I(s_{t};\theta\mid h_{t},a_{t:T},s_{Z}) is the epistemic residual.

Step 2: Isolating the Abductive Bias.
The abductive term AZA_{Z} captures dependencies generated purely by the known transition kernel, relying on the prior p⁡(θ)p(\theta) only through the posterior p⁡(θ∣ht)p(\theta\mid h_{t}). We may evaluate the limit on an environment M∈ℳM\in\mathcal{M} whose prior is a degenerate point mass at some θ∗\theta^{*}. For such a prior, there is no uncertainty about the environment, so the true Bayesian Information Gain I⁡(st;θ∣ht)=0I(s_{t};\theta\mid h_{t})=0 and all epistemic residuals EZ=0E_{Z}=0 identically. The universal convergence hypothesis then reduces to:

limT→∞∑ZcZ,T​AZ​(θ∗)=0for every ​θ∗.\lim_{T\to\infty}\sum_{Z}c_{Z,T}A_{Z}(\theta^{*})=0\quad\text{for every }\theta^{*}\,. (7)

Step 3: The Markov Funnel.
Under assumption (i), conditional on the exact parameter θ∗\theta^{*}, the environment is Markovian. By the data-processing inequality, the dependence of any block sZs_{Z} on the state sts_{t} must funnel strictly through the chronologically earliest state in that block, st+kZs_{t+k_{Z}}. Dropping the separated future actions, we have:

AZ(θ∗)=I(st;st+kZ∣θ∗,ht,at:t+kZ−1)≔IkZ(θ∗).A_{Z}(\theta^{*})=I(s_{t};s_{t+k_{Z}}\mid\theta^{*},h_{t},a_{t:t+k_{Z}-1})\coloneqq I_{k_{Z}}(\theta^{*})\,.

limT→∞∑k=1TWk,T​Ik​(θ∗)=0for every ​θ∗.\lim_{T\to\infty}\sum_{k=1}^{T}W_{k,T}I_{k}(\theta^{*})=0\quad\text{for every }\theta^{*}\,. (8)

Step 4: AR(1) Instantiation and Power Series Extraction.
To evaluate equation 8, we instantiate MM with the Gaussian AR(1) family parameterized by α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1), for which the mutual information across a gap kk is Ik​(α)=−12​log⁡(1−α2​k)I_{k}(\alpha)=-\frac{1}{2}\log(1-\alpha^{2k}). Letting x=α2∈(0,1)x=\alpha^{2}\in(0,1), we define the sequence of functions:

FT​(x)≔∑k=1TWk,T​(−log⁡(1−xk)).F_{T}(x)\coloneqq\sum_{k=1}^{T}W_{k,T}\big(-\log(1-x^{k})\big)\,.

By hypothesis, limT→∞FT​(x)=0\lim_{T\to\infty}F_{T}(x)=0 for all x∈(0,1)x\in(0,1). We extend FT​(x)F_{T}(x) to the complex plane as FT​(z)F_{T}(z), which is analytic on the open unit disk |z|<1|z|<1. Expanding the principal branch of the logarithm in its Maclaurin series −log⁡(1−zk)=∑m=1∞zk​mm-\log(1-z^{k})=\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}\frac{z^{km}}{m}, we express FT​(z)F_{T}(z) as:

FT​(z)=∑k=1TWk,T​∑m=1∞zk​mm=∑n=1∞Vn,Tn​zn,F_{T}(z)=\sum_{k=1}^{T}W_{k,T}\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}\frac{z^{km}}{m}=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{V_{n,T}}{n}z^{n}\,,

where we have grouped terms by n=k​mn=km and defined Vn,T≔∑d|n,d<Td​Wd,TV_{n,T}\coloneqq\sum_{d|n,\;d<T}dW_{d,T}.

Now recall that the theorem statement assumes that there exist constants C>0C>0 and B≥1B\geq 1 such that |Wk,T|≤∑kZ=k|cZ,T|≤C​Bk|W_{k,T}|\leq\sum_{k_{Z}=k}|c_{Z,T}|\leq CB^{k} for all kk and TT. Applying our exponential bound to the weights yields:

|FT​(z)|≤∑k=1T|Wk,T|​|−log⁡(1−zk)|≤C1−|z|​∑k=1∞(B​|z|)k.|F_{T}(z)|\leq\sum_{k=1}^{T}|W_{k,T}|\,|-\log(1-z^{k})|\leq\frac{C}{1-|z|}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}(B|z|)^{k}\,.

This geometric series converges absolutely for B​|z|<1B|z|<1. Thus, defining a bounding radius R≔min⁡(1/2,1/B)R\coloneqq\min(1/2,1/B), the sequence of functions {FT​(z)}\{F_{T}(z)\} is uniformly bounded by a finite constant on any closed ball B⁡(0,r)B(0,r) with r<Rr<R.

Because FT​(x)→0F_{T}(x)\to 0 pointwise on the real interval (0,R)(0,R), and this interval contains an accumulation point strictly within B⁡(0,R)B(0,R), the Vitali-Porter Convergence Theorem (Schiff, 1993, Section 2.4) guarantees that FT​(z)F_{T}(z) converges uniformly to 00 on any strictly smaller closed contour γ\gamma enclosing the origin. By Cauchy’s Integral Formula, the nn-th Maclaurin coefficient is given by:

Vn,Tn=12​π​i​∮γFT​(z)zn+1​𝑑z.\frac{V_{n,T}}{n}=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_{\gamma}\frac{F_{T}(z)}{z^{n+1}}\mathrm{d}z\,.

limT→∞Vn,Tn=0⟹limT→∞Vn,T=0for all ​n≥1.\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{V_{n,T}}{n}=0\implies\lim_{T\to\infty}V_{n,T}=0\quad\text{for all }n\geq 1\,.

Step 5: Strong Induction.
We prove limT→∞Wk,T=0\lim_{T\to\infty}W_{k,T}=0 by strong induction on kk. For the base case k=1k=1, we have V1,T=W1,TV_{1,T}=W_{1,T} (since d<Td<T trivially for T>1T>1), and thus limT→∞W1,T=0\lim_{T\to\infty}W_{1,T}=0. For the inductive step, assume that limT→∞Wd,T=0\lim_{T\to\infty}W_{d,T}=0 for all proper divisors d<nd<n. By definition, for T>nT>n:

Vn,T=n​Wn,T+∑d|nd<nd​Wd,T.V_{n,T}=nW_{n,T}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}d|n\\ d<n\end{subarray}}dW_{d,T}\,.

Taking the limit as T→∞T\to\infty:

0=n​limT→∞Wn,T+∑d|nd<nd​(limT→∞Wd,T)⏟=0⟹limT→∞Wn,T=0.0=n\lim_{T\to\infty}W_{n,T}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}d|n\\ d<n\end{subarray}}d\underbrace{\Big(\lim_{T\to\infty}W_{d,T}\Big)}_{=0}\implies\lim_{T\to\infty}W_{n,T}=0\,.

This holds for all integers n≥1n\geq 1, proving that all finite gap weights strictly vanish as T→∞T\to\infty. Consequently, any estimator universally approaching BIG must concentrate its weight strictly at an unbounded, infinite gap.

∎

Remark (relation to Theorem 1).

The earlier impossibility theorem covers ℱ\mathcal{F} at every finite touch horizon QQ: at finite TT, no member of ℱ\mathcal{F} identifies BIG, even without log-ratio structure. Theorem 7 extends the negative result into the limit: even allowing countable log-ratio combinations and asymptotic TT, the only escape is a structural double limit in which both the gap and the block grow without bound. As mentioned in the main text, this imposes severe implementation limitations since predictive models ρ\rho are well suited for long sequence modeling (large TT) but less so for marginalization over unobserved sequence blocks (large gaps).

C.9 Proof of Corollary 3.1

See 3.1

Proof.

Under BED structure, given θ\theta and the action sequence, st∼p(⋅∣at−1,θ)s_{t}\sim p(\cdot\mid a_{t-1},\theta) and st+1∼p(⋅∣at,θ)s_{t+1}\sim p(\cdot\mid a_{t},\theta) are independent. Hence I(st;st+1∣θ,ht,at)=0I(s_{t};s_{t+1}\mid\theta,h_{t},a_{t})=0, and the abductive term in Theorem 3 drops out. ∎

C.10 Proof of Theorem 4

See 4

Proof.

Under BED, p⁡(st∣st−1,at−1,θ)=p⁡(st∣at−1,θ)p(s_{t}\mid s_{t-1},a_{t-1},\theta)=p(s_{t}\mid a_{t-1},\theta), so the integral in Equation 4 simplifies:

∫p⁡(st∣at−1,θ)​p​(θ∣ht,st)​𝑑θ=𝔼p⁡(θ∣ht,st)​[p⁡(st∣at−1,θ)]=ρ⁡(st∣ht)​𝔼p⁡(θ∣ht,st)​[L⁡(θ)],\int p(s_{t}\mid a_{t-1},\theta)\,p(\theta\mid h_{t},s_{t})\,d\theta\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{p(\theta\mid h_{t},s_{t})}[p(s_{t}\mid a_{t-1},\theta)]\;=\;\rho(s_{t}\mid h_{t})\,\mathbb{E}_{p(\theta\mid h_{t},s_{t})}[L(\theta)],

where the last equality uses the definition L⁡(θ)=p⁡(st∣at−1,θ)/ρ⁡(st∣ht)L(\theta)=p(s_{t}\mid a_{t-1},\theta)/\rho(s_{t}\mid h_{t}). Hence

rtdl=log⁡𝔼p⁡(θ∣ht,st)​[L⁡(θ)].r^{\mathrm{dl}}_{t}\;=\;\log\mathbb{E}_{p(\theta\mid h_{t},s_{t})}[L(\theta)].

By Jensen’s inequality,

rtdl=𝔼p⁡(θ∣ht,st)​[log⁡L⁡(θ)]+𝒥t,r^{\mathrm{dl}}_{t}\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{p(\theta\mid h_{t},s_{t})}[\log L(\theta)]+\mathcal{J}_{t},

with 𝒥t≥0\mathcal{J}_{t}\geq 0 the Jensen gap. Bayes’ rule gives L⁡(θ)=p⁡(θ∣ht,st)/p⁡(θ∣ht)L(\theta)=p(\theta\mid h_{t},s_{t})/p(\theta\mid h_{t}), so 𝔼p⁡(θ∣ht,st)[logL(θ)]=DKL(p(θ∣ht,st)∥p(θ∣ht))\mathbb{E}_{p(\theta\mid h_{t},s_{t})}[\log L(\theta)]=D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\bigl(p(\theta\mid h_{t},s_{t})\,\|\,p(\theta\mid h_{t})\bigr). Taking expectation over sts_{t}, the KL term integrates to I⁡(st;θ∣ht)I(s_{t};\theta\mid h_{t}) (Bayesian-surprise identity). ∎

Remark.

Theorem 4 shows an important limitation of rdlr^{\mathrm{dl}}. While technically, rdlr^{\mathrm{dl}} does recover BIG asymptotically, it does so as t→∞t\to\infty which also implies that BIG I⁡(st;θ∣ht)I(s_{t};\theta\mid h_{t}) itself vanishes. This means that rdlr^{\mathrm{dl}} biases vanish at the same time as the BIG signal itself does. In contrast, rsumr^{\mathrm{sum}} also recovers BIG asymptotically, but it does so as T→∞T\to\infty, meaning that for long trajectories, one can hope to recover minimally biased BIG signal for finite tt. However, the practical effect of finite-time biases may or may not be consequential for a useful policy, depending on the environment. Experiments in the main text illustrate this point.

Appendix D Implementing rdlr^{\mathrm{dl}} in General BAMDPs vs. BED

The reward rdlr^{\mathrm{dl}} defined in Equation 4 contains an integral term

∫p⁡(st∣st−1,at−1,θ)​p​(θ∣ht,st)​𝑑θ\int p(s_{t}\mid s_{t-1},a_{t-1},\theta)\,p(\theta\mid h_{t},s_{t})\,d\theta

that pairs the kernel at the trajectory input (st−1,at−1)(s_{t-1},a_{t-1}) with a posterior conditioned on the subsequent observation sts_{t}. We explain here why this combination is generically not implementable through ρ\rho’s standard predictive interface, and how the BED restriction restores implementability via a counterfactual action commitment.

Why no ρ\rho-implementation in general BAMDPs.

A standard ρ\rho query ρ⁡(s′∣h)\rho(s^{\prime}\mid h) evaluates the kernel at the most recent (s,a)(s,a) in the conditioning history hh, averaged under the posterior p⁡(θ∣h)p(\theta\mid h) that this same history induces. The integrand above departs from this template in a structural way: the kernel input is (st−1,at−1)(s_{t-1},a_{t-1}) from time t−1t-1, while the posterior is p⁡(θ∣ht,st)p(\theta\mid h_{t},s_{t}) from after sts_{t} has been observed. In a general MDP, where the kernel genuinely depends on the chain-position state, no rearrangement of conditioning subsets in ρ\rho’s query interface produces this combination — evaluating ρ\rho at (st−1,at−1)(s_{t-1},a_{t-1}) gives the posterior only up to time t−1t-1, and evaluating ρ\rho after sts_{t} shifts the kernel input as well. Implementing rdlr^{\mathrm{dl}} in general BAMDPs therefore requires explicit Bayesian-update machinery beyond ρ\rho’s forward-pass interface.

BED counterfactual identity.

In BED the transition kernel has no st−1s_{t-1} dependence, p⁡(st∣st−1,at−1,θ)=p⁡(st∣at−1,θ)p(s_{t}\mid s_{t-1},a_{t-1},\theta)=p(s_{t}\mid a_{t-1},\theta), so the integrand becomes

∫p⁡(st∣at−1,θ)​p​(θ∣ht,st)​𝑑θ=ρ⁡(st+1=st|ht,st,at=at−1),\int p(s_{t}\mid a_{t-1},\theta)\,p(\theta\mid h_{t},s_{t})\,d\theta\;=\;\rho\bigl(s_{t+1}=s_{t}\,\big|\,h_{t},s_{t},\,a_{t}=a_{t-1}\bigr),

recovering Equation 6. The right-hand side is a standard ρ\rho query: condition on the history (ht,st)(h_{t},s_{t}), commit to the action at=at−1a_{t}=a_{t-1} (a counterfactual on the action choice, valid because actions are policy-generated and thus interventional), and read off the predictive probability of the next outcome equaling the observed sts_{t}. This makes rdlr^{\mathrm{dl}} implementable in BED at the cost of one hypothetical rollout step in ρ\rho’s context.

The key takeaway: BED collapses the chain-time mismatch by removing the st−1s_{t-1} dependence in the kernel — an obstruction that no rearrangement of ρ\rho’s queries can resolve in a general MDP. It could be possible to address this issue with a modified sequence model architecture that allows multiple channels for the same sequence location, together with a gating mechanism to implement a form of counterfactual “superposition”. This remains a non-trivial design.

Appendix E Experimental Details

E.1 Gaussian Processes

E.1.1 Environment

The Gaussian Process (GP) environment presents the agent with an unknown function f:ℝ2→ℝf:\mathbb{R}^{2}\to\mathbb{R} that must be explored through sequential point queries. At the start of each episode, a function ff is sampled from a Gaussian process prior f∼𝒢​𝒫​(0,k)f\sim\mathcal{GP}(0,k), where kk is the rational quadratic kernel:

k⁡(𝐱,𝐱′)=σ2​(1+‖𝐱−𝐱′‖22​α​ℓ2)−α,k(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})=\sigma^{2}\left(1+\frac{\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\|^{2}}{2\alpha\ell^{2}}\right)^{-\alpha}, (9)

with α=1\alpha=1, lengthscale ℓ=4.0\ell=4.0, and σ2=1\sigma^{2}=1.

Since a GP sample is an infinite-dimensional function, we represent it in practice via finite-grid sampling: we place R=10R=10 equally spaced points along each of the dd input dimensions in [−xmax,,xmax][-x_{\max},,x_{\max}] and take their Cartesian product, yielding a grid 𝐗g​r​i​d\mathbf{X}_{grid} of N=RdN=R^{d} locations. To draw a sample 𝐲grid\mathbf{y}_{\mathrm{grid}} from this multivariate Gaussian we use the standard Cholesky method. Function values at arbitrary query points are then obtained via GP posterior interpolation. We use xmax=10x_{\max}=10.

When the agent queries location 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t}, it observes:

yt=f⁡(𝐱t)+ϵt,ϵt∼𝒩⁡(0,σnoise2​(𝐱t)),y_{t}=f(\mathbf{x}_{t})+\epsilon_{t},\qquad\epsilon_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}\bigl(0,\sigma_{\text{noise}}^{2}(\mathbf{x}_{t})\bigr), (10)

where the noise variance σnoise2​(𝐱)\sigma_{\text{noise}}^{2}(\mathbf{x}) is spatially varying according to a fixed checkerboard noise map. 𝐗g​r​i​d\mathbf{X}_{grid} is partitioned into an 8×88\times 8 grid of cells; Tiles alternate between high-noise (σnoise2=5\sigma_{\mathrm{noise}}^{2}=5) and low-noise (σnoise2≈0\sigma_{\mathrm{noise}}^{2}\approx 0) regions. This creates a heteroscedastic noise landscape that an effective exploration policy must learn to navigate.

E.1.2 Bayesian Oracle World Model

The Bayesian oracle leverages the closed-form GP posterior. Given a history of observations {(𝐱i,yi)}i=0t−1\{(\mathbf{x}_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=0}^{t-1}, the posterior predictive distribution for a new query 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t} is Gaussian:

p⁡(yt∣𝐱t,ht)=𝒩⁡(yt,μt,σt2),p(y_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t},h_{t})=\mathcal{N}\bigl(y_{t};\,\mu_{t},\sigma_{t}^{2}\bigr), (11)

where the posterior mean and variance are given by the standard GP regression formulae:

μt\displaystyle\mu_{t} =𝐤∗⊤​(K+Σnoise)−1​𝐲<t,\displaystyle=\mathbf{k}_{*}^{\top}(K+\Sigma_{\text{noise}})^{-1}\mathbf{y}_{<t}, (12)
σt2\displaystyle\sigma_{t}^{2} =k⁡(𝐱t,𝐱t)−𝐤∗⊤​(K+Σnoise)−1​𝐤∗,\displaystyle=k(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{x}_{t})-\mathbf{k}_{*}^{\top}(K+\Sigma_{\text{noise}})^{-1}\mathbf{k}_{*}, (13)

with 𝐤∗=[k⁡(𝐱i,𝐱t)]i=0t−1\mathbf{k}_{*}=[k(\mathbf{x}_{i},\mathbf{x}_{t})]_{i=0}^{t-1}, Ki​j=k⁡(𝐱i,𝐱j)K_{ij}=k(\mathbf{x}_{i},\mathbf{x}_{j}), and Σnoise=diag⁡(σnoise2​(𝐱0),…,σnoise2​(𝐱t−1))\Sigma_{\text{noise}}=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_{\text{noise}}^{2}(\mathbf{x}_{0}),\ldots,\sigma_{\text{noise}}^{2}(\mathbf{x}_{t-1})).

For the predictive distribution used by the surprisal-based rewards, the predictive variance additionally includes the noise at the query point:

σ~t2=σt2+σnoise2​(𝐱t).\tilde{\sigma}_{t}^{2}=\sigma_{t}^{2}+\sigma_{\text{noise}}^{2}(\mathbf{x}_{t}). (14)
Per-step Surprisal

The observation surprisal is the negative log-likelihood under the predictive Gaussian:

−log⁡p⁡(yt∣𝐱t,ht)=12​log⁡(2​π)+12​log⁡σ~t2+(yt−μt)22​σ~t2.-\log p(y_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t},h_{t})=\frac{1}{2}\log(2\pi)+\frac{1}{2}\log\tilde{\sigma}_{t}^{2}+\frac{(y_{t}-\mu_{t})^{2}}{2\tilde{\sigma}_{t}^{2}}. (15)
Per-step Information Gain (Bayesian Surprise)

The information gain reward uses the KL divergence between the GP posterior and the predictive observation distribution. In exact form:

Gt=12​log⁡(1+σt2σnoise2​(𝐱t))−σt22​(σt2+σnoise2​(𝐱t))+σt2⋅(yt−μt)22​(σt2+σnoise2​(𝐱t))2,\text{G}_{t}=\frac{1}{2}\log\!\left(1+\frac{\sigma_{t}^{2}}{\sigma_{\text{noise}}^{2}(\mathbf{x}_{t})}\right)-\frac{\sigma_{t}^{2}}{2(\sigma_{t}^{2}+\sigma_{\text{noise}}^{2}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))}+\frac{\sigma_{t}^{2}\cdot(y_{t}-\mu_{t})^{2}}{2(\sigma_{t}^{2}+\sigma_{\text{noise}}^{2}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))^{2}}, (16)

where σt2\sigma_{t}^{2} is the latent GP posterior variance (without observation noise).

E.1.3 In-Context PFN World Model

Data-Generating Process

The PFN is trained to predict the next observation yty_{t} in-context from the history of observed pairs. For each training example, a function ff is sampled from the same GP prior as the environment (rational quadratic kernel with α=1\alpha=1, ℓ=4.0\ell=4.0, spatially-varying noise), and Ttrain=100T_{\text{train}}=100 random query locations are drawn uniformly from [−10,10]2[-10,10]^{2}.

Model Architecture

The PFN uses a causal Transformer decoder. Each past observation (xj,yj)(x_{j},y_{j}) is embedded by summing a linear projection of xjx_{j} and a linear projection of yjy_{j} into a single “pair” token. This pair token is interleaved with an isolated embedding of the next query xj+1x_{j+1}, yielding a sequence of length 2​(t−1)2(t{-}1). The causal Transformer decoder has model dimension d=512d=512, MLP hidden dimension F=1024F=1024, N=12N=12 layers, and H=8H=8 attention heads with head dimension d/H=64d/H=64. The model uses LayerNorm and GELU activations. The Transformer output at each query-token position (odd positions) is projected via a learned linear layer to produce a 22-dimensional output (μ^t,σ^t)(\hat{\mu}_{t},\hat{\sigma}_{t}), representing a predicted mean and log-standard-deviation.

Training

The training objective is the mean negative log-likelihood of the observed yy values under the predicted Gaussian, with a variance-weighted loss to encourage better calibration (Seitzer et al., 2022):

ℒ=1(T−1)​B​∑b=1B∑t=1T−1[sg⁡(σ^t2)]β⋅[12​log⁡(2​π​σ^t2)+(yt−μ^t)22​σ^t2],\mathcal{L}=\frac{1}{(T-1)B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\bigl[\operatorname{sg}(\hat{\sigma}_{t}^{2})\bigr]^{\beta}\cdot\left[\frac{1}{2}\log(2\pi\hat{\sigma}_{t}^{2})+\frac{(y_{t}-\hat{\mu}_{t})^{2}}{2\hat{\sigma}_{t}^{2}}\right], (17)

where sg⁡(⋅)\operatorname{sg}(\cdot) denotes stop-gradient, σ^t2=exp⁡(2​σ^t)\hat{\sigma}_{t}^{2}=\exp(2\hat{\sigma}_{t}) is the predicted variance, and β=1\beta=1. The model is optimized using Adam with a learning rate of 10−410^{-4}, batch size B=128B=128, for 10610^{6} training steps.

We collect random trajectories from Gaussian processes, and plot the correlation between the predictions of the Bayesian oracle world model and the trained PFN world model in Figure E.1. The trained PFN is effective at approximating the exact likelihood and, as evidenced by other results, is effective even in settings where the oracle cannot be computed.

E.1.4 Policy

The policy is trained using REINFORCE with a learned value baseline. At each training step, B=32B=32 trajectories of length T=26T=26 are collected by rolling out the current policy in the environment. A single trajectory-level reward RR is computed from the world model, and the policy is updated with a single gradient step per batch. The REINFORCE objective combines a policy gradient loss and a value baseline loss:

ℒ=ℒπ+λV​ℒV,\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\pi}+\lambda_{V}\mathcal{L}_{V}, (18)

where λV=0.5\lambda_{V}=0.5.

Model Architecture

The policy is a sequence model that processes the history of observations recurrently. The backbone is a Griffin model (De et al., 2024), a recurrent architecture based on linear recurrences (LRU). The Griffin configuration uses model dimension d=128d=128, MLP dimension 256256, LRU dimension 128128, 44 attention heads, and 22 recurrent layers.

At each step tt, the observation ot=(𝐱t,yt)o_{t}=(\mathbf{x}_{t},y_{t}) is encoded by concatenating 𝐱t∈ℝ2\mathbf{x}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{2} and yt∈ℝy_{t}\in\mathbb{R}, yielding a 3-dimensional vector, which is projected to the model dimension d=128d=128 via a learned linear layer.

The sequence model output at each step is mapped to logits over the 6464 discrete grid locations via a single linear layer. A separate linear layer maps the sequence model output to a scalar value estimate V⁡(st)∈ℝV(s_{t})\in\mathbb{R}.

E.2 Decomposition of rewards

In Section 4.3, we analyzed the theoretical behaviour of curiosity rewards in BED environments. Corollary 3.1 showed that rsumr^{\mathrm{sum}} decomposes into BIG−Residual\text{BIG}-\text{Residual} terms, while Theorem 4 showed that rdlr^{\mathrm{dl}} decomposes into BIG+JensenGap\text{BIG}+\text{JensenGap} terms. In our Gaussian process environment using an Bayesian oracle observer, all terms can be computed analytically. After having trained a policy with either rsumr^{\mathrm{sum}} or rdlr^{\mathrm{dl}}, we can therefore check whether the reward empirically decomposes into the expected terms that our theory predicts.

Figure E.3 plots the resulting reward, BIG, and nuisance term as a function of time, averaged across 10 training seeds and 1000 unrolled trajectories. We find that both rewards decompose exactly into their theoretical constituents, thus validating our theoretical analyses. Indeed, plotting BIG−Residual\text{BIG}-\text{Residual} overlaps exactly with rsumr^{\mathrm{sum}}, and plotting BIG+JensenGap\text{BIG}+\text{JensenGap} overlaps exactly with rdlr^{\mathrm{dl}}.

E.3 Mastermind

At the start of each episode, the environment samples a secret code 𝐜∗∈{0,1,…,C−1}L\mathbf{c}^{*}\in\{0,1,\ldots,C-1\}^{L} uniformly at random, where CC is the number of colours and LL is the code length. In our experiments we set C=6C=6 and L=7L=7, yielding 67=279,9366^{7}=279{,}936 possible codes. We hold out 10% of the possible codes for evaluation.

At each timestep tt, the agent submits a guess 𝐠t∈{0,1,…,C−1}L\mathbf{g}_{t}\in\{0,1,\ldots,C-1\}^{L} and receives a response (bt,wt)(b_{t},w_{t}) where:

  • •

    Black peg bt∈{0,…,L}b_{t}\in\{0,\ldots,L\} is the number of exact matches (correct colour in the correct position), and

  • •

    White peg wt∈{0,…,L}w_{t}\in\{0,\ldots,L\} is the number of colour matches (correct colour regardless of position), computed as wt=∑c=0C−1min⁡(count​(c,𝐜∗),count​(c,𝐠t))w_{t}=\sum_{c=0}^{C-1}\min\!\bigl(\text{count}(c,\mathbf{c}^{*}),\,\text{count}(c,\mathbf{g}_{t})\bigr), where count​(c,𝐯)\text{count}(c,\mathbf{v}) is the number of occurrences of colour cc in vector 𝐯\mathbf{v}.

Note that wt≥btw_{t}\geq b_{t} always holds, and colours are not double-counted: if the code contains NN repeats of a colour but the guess has M>NM>N entries of that colour, only NN contribute to wtw_{t}.

The episode proceeds for a fixed trajectory length of T=8T=8 guesses. A random initial guess is generated at the start of each episode and forms the first observation.

E.3.1 Bayesian Oracle World Model

The Bayesian oracle world model maintains the exact posterior over secret codes by enumerating over all CLC^{L} possible codes. Given a history of guesses and responses {(𝐠1,b1,w1),…,(𝐠t−1,bt−1,wt−1)}\{(\mathbf{g}_{1},b_{1},w_{1}),\ldots,(\mathbf{g}_{t-1},b_{t-1},w_{t-1})\}, the oracle computes the set of consistent codes—those that would have produced the observed responses for all past guesses. Formally, a code 𝐜\mathbf{c} is consistent at step tt if for all i<ti<t: exact​(𝐜,𝐠i)=bi\text{exact}(\mathbf{c},\mathbf{g}_{i})=b_{i} and colour​(𝐜,𝐠i)=wi\text{colour}(\mathbf{c},\mathbf{g}_{i})=w_{i}.

The uniform prior over codes, combined with consistency filtering, yields the posterior probability of a newly observed response (bt,wt)(b_{t},w_{t}) given a new guess 𝐠t\mathbf{g}_{t} as:

p(bt,wt∣ht=[ht−1,st−1,𝐠t])=|{𝐜∈𝒞t:exact​(𝐜,𝐠t)=bt∧colour​(𝐜,𝐠t)=wt}||𝒞t|,p(b_{t},w_{t}\mid h_{t}=[h_{t-1},s_{t-1},\mathbf{g}_{t}])=\frac{|\{\mathbf{c}\in\mathcal{C}_{t}:\text{exact}(\mathbf{c},\mathbf{g}_{t})=b_{t}\wedge\text{colour}(\mathbf{c},\mathbf{g}_{t})=w_{t}\}|}{|\mathcal{C}_{t}|}, (19)

where 𝒞t\mathcal{C}_{t} denotes the set of codes consistent with all observations prior to step tt.

E.3.2 In-Context PFN World Model

Data-Generating Process

The PFN is trained on synthetically generated game trajectories. For each training example, a secret code is sampled uniformly at random, and then a sequence of Ttrain=50T_{\text{train}}=50 random guesses is generated. Each guess is drawn uniformly from {0,…,C−1}L\{0,\ldots,C-1\}^{L}, and the corresponding responses (bt,wt)(b_{t},w_{t}) are computed by the environment.

Model Architecture

The in-context world model is a causal Transformer decoder that processes interleaved guess and response tokens. Specifically, each guess 𝐠t\mathbf{g}_{t} is one-hot encoded over the CC colours for each of the LL positions, yielding a vector of dimension C×LC\times L, which is then projected to the model dimension dd via a linear layer. Each response (bt,wt)(b_{t},w_{t}) is one-hot encoded as a concatenation of two vectors of dimension (L+1)(L+1) each, giving a total dimension of 2​(L+1)2(L+1), which is projected to dd via a separate linear layer. For a trajectory of TT steps, the input sequence is constructed by interleaving pairs and isolated guesses. A pair token is formed by summing the guess and response embeddings for the same timestep: 𝐩t=embedg​(𝐠t)+embedr​(bt,wt)\mathbf{p}_{t}=\text{embed}_{g}(\mathbf{g}_{t})+\text{embed}_{r}(b_{t},w_{t}). The isolated guess token for the next step is embedg​(𝐠t+1)\text{embed}_{g}(\mathbf{g}_{t+1}). These are interleaved as [𝐩1,embedg​(𝐠2),𝐩2,embedg​(𝐠3),…][\mathbf{p}_{1},\text{embed}_{g}(\mathbf{g}_{2}),\mathbf{p}_{2},\text{embed}_{g}(\mathbf{g}_{3}),\ldots], resulting in a sequence of length 2​(T−1)2(T-1).

The sequence is processed by a causal (left-to-right) Transformer decoder with the model dimension d=512d=512, MLP hidden dimension = 1024, 12 layers, and 8 attention heads with head dimension = 64. The Transformer output at every odd position (i.e., the isolated guess positions) is used to predict the corresponding response. A linear readout maps the Transformer output to (L+1)2(L+1)^{2} logits, representing the joint distribution over all possible (bt,wt)(b_{t},w_{t}) pairs via a softmax. The target is the index bt⋅(L+1)+wtb_{t}\cdot(L+1)+w_{t}.

The in-context world model is trained to minimize the cross-entropy loss of predicting the response at each step. In each training step, a fresh batch of B=128B=128 random trajectories is generated on-the-fly (no fixed dataset).

E.3.3 Policy

The policy is trained using REINFORCE with a learned value baseline. At each training step, a batch of B=32B=32 trajectories of length T=8T=8 is collected by rolling out the current policy in the environment. The total loss for REINFORCE is:

ℒ=ℒπ+λV​ℒV,\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\pi}+\lambda_{V}\mathcal{L}_{V}, (20)

where λV=0.5\lambda_{V}=0.5. When using the in-context world model (PFN observer), an entropy bonus −λH​ℋ​[πϕ]-\lambda_{H}\mathcal{H}[\pi_{\phi}] with λH=0.01\lambda_{H}=0.01 is added to the loss to encourage exploration.

Model Architecture

The policy model’s backbone is a Griffin model with the same configuration as the one for GP. The guess 𝐠t\mathbf{g}_{t} is one-hot encoded over the CC colours for each position, yielding a vector of dimension C×LC\times L. The exact matches btb_{t} and colour matches wtw_{t} are each one-hot encoded into vectors of dimension L+1L+1. These are concatenated into a single vector of dimension C⋅L+2​(L+1)C\cdot L+2(L+1) and projected to the model dimension dd via a linear layer.

The policy produces a value estimate and an action distribution. A linear layer maps the sequence model output at each step to a scalar value estimate V⁡(st)V(s_{t}). The action (a guess of LL colour values) is generated autoregressively, one position at a time, using a GRU cell. At each position k∈{1,…,L}k\in\{1,\ldots,L\}:

  1. 1.

    The GRU cell updates its hidden state using the current input (the sequence model output for k=1k=1, or the embedding of the previously selected colour for k>1k>1).

  2. 2.

    A linear readout produces logits over the CC colours for position kk.

  3. 3.

    A colour is sampled from Categorical​(softmax​(logitsk/τ))\text{Categorical}(\text{softmax}(\text{logits}_{k}/\tau)), where τ\tau is the temperature (set to 1.01.0 during training).

  4. 4.

    The selected colour is embedded and fed as input to the GRU for the next position.

The log-probability of the full action is the sum of the per-position log-probabilities: logπ(at∣st)=∑k=1Llogπk(at(k)∣st,at(1:k−1))\log\pi(a_{t}\mid s_{t})=\sum_{k=1}^{L}\log\pi_{k}(a_{t}^{(k)}\mid s_{t},a_{t}^{(1:k-1)}).

E.4 Alchemy

The Alchemy environment is inspired by the latent-chemistry paradigm of Wang et al. (2021). At the start of each episode, an environment is sampled with a hidden chemistry: a set of deterministic transition rules governing how potions transform stones. Stones are described by D=4D=4 discrete dimensions with value counts (3,3,3,4)(3,3,3,4), yielding 3×3×3×4=1083\times 3\times 3\times 4=108 distinct stone types. Potions are described by a single discrete dimension with P=6P=6 values. Each chemistry defines a fixed mapping from (initial_stone, potion) pairs to resulting stones; if a given (stone, potion) pair has no matching rule, the stone is returned unchanged and the transition is marked as invalid. The full set of chemistries and their transition rules are stored as a precomputed transition table of shape [Nenvs,Nrules,2​D+P][N_{\text{envs}},N_{\text{rules}},2D+P].

At each timestep tt, the agent chooses an action at=(it,pt)a_{t}=(i_{t},p_{t})—an initial stone and a potion—and the environment returns an observation (vt,ft)(v_{t},f_{t}) where vt∈{0,1}v_{t}\in\{0,1\} indicates whether the transition was valid (i.e., a matching rule exists in the current chemistry), and ftf_{t} is the resulting stone (equal to iti_{t} when vt=0v_{t}=0).

The episode proceeds for a fixed trajectory length of T=5T=5 steps. A random initial transition is sampled from the environment’s transition table at the start of each episode and forms the first observation.

E.4.1 Bayesian Oracle World Model

Similar to Mastermind, the Bayesian oracle world model maintains the exact posterior over hidden chemistries by enumerating all NenvsN_{\text{envs}} candidate environments. Given a history of observations, the oracle computes a consistency mask: a candidate chemistry θ\theta is consistent at step tt if, for all prior observations (it′,pt′,vt′,ft′)(i_{t^{\prime}},p_{t^{\prime}},v_{t^{\prime}},f_{t^{\prime}}) with t′<t{t^{\prime}}<t:

  1. 1.

    If vt′=1v_{t^{\prime}}=1: chemistry θ\theta contains a rule (it′,pt′)↦ft′(i_{t^{\prime}},p_{t^{\prime}})\mapsto f_{t^{\prime}} that produces the observed output stone, and

  2. 2.

    If vt′=0v_{t^{\prime}}=0: chemistry θ\theta has no rule matching the input pair (it′,pt′)(i_{t^{\prime}},p_{t^{\prime}}).

The posterior probability of a new observation st=(vt,ft)s_{t}=(v_{t},f_{t}) is computed as:

ρ(st∣ht=[ht−1,st−1,(it,pT)])=|{e∈ℰt:e​ is consistent with ​(it,pt,vt,ft)}||ℰt|,\rho(s_{t}\mid h_{t}=[h_{t-1},s_{t-1},(i_{t},p_{T})])=\frac{\bigl|\{e\in\mathcal{E}_{t}:e\text{ is consistent with }(i_{t},p_{t},v_{t},f_{t})\}\bigr|}{|\mathcal{E}_{t}|}, (21)

where ℰt\mathcal{E}_{t} denotes the set of chemistries consistent with all observations prior to step tt.

This world model provides exact Bayesian inference but scales linearly in the number of candidate environments, which must be enumerated exhaustively.

E.4.2 In-Context PFN World Model

The world model is a 12-layer causal Transformer with model dimension d=512d{=}512, 8 attention heads, and feed-forward dimension 10241024. Each observation ot=(it,pt,ft)o_{t}=(i_{t},p_{t},f_{t}) is split into an input token (encoding iti_{t} and ptp_{t} via concatenated one-hot vectors, projected to ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}) and an output token (encoding ftf_{t} similarly). These are interleaved into a sequence [in1,out1,in2,out2,…][\text{in}_{1},\text{out}_{1},\text{in}_{2},\text{out}_{2},\dots] of length 2​T2T and processed with causal attention, so that the hidden state at each input position int\text{in}_{t} attends to all tokens up to and including outt−1\text{out}_{t-1}.

The output prediction head is an autoregressive GRU decoder that, starting from the Transformer’s hidden state at int\text{in}_{t}, sequentially predicts each component of the observation output: first a validity flag (2 categories), then each of the four stone dimensions (3, 3, 3, and 4 categories respectively). At each step the GRU receives the embedding of the previous ground-truth component (teacher forcing during training), updates its hidden state, and produces logits over the current component’s categories. Invalid logit positions (where the category index exceeds the component’s vocabulary) are masked to −∞-\infty before the softmax.

The model is trained on sequences of Ttrain=50T_{\mathrm{train}}{=}50 transitions sampled with uniformly random actions from uniformly sampled environment IDs, with batch size B=64B{=}64 and the Adam optimizer at learning rate 10−410^{-4}.

Data-Generating Process

The PFN is trained on synthetically generated transition trajectories. For each training example, a chemistry (environment) is sampled uniformly at random, and then a sequence of Ttrain=20T_{\text{train}}=20 random transitions is generated. Each transition draws a random initial stone and potion uniformly from their respective value ranges, and the corresponding observation (vt,stout)(v_{t},\textbf{s}_{t}^{\text{out}}) is computed by the environment.

Model Architecture

The in-context world model is a causal Transformer decoder that processes interleaved input (action) and output (observation) tokens. Each input token encodes the initial stone and potion via per-dimension one-hot vectors. The stone dimensions (3,3,3,4)(3,3,3,4) and potion dimension (6)(6) are each one-hot encoded and concatenated, yielding a vector of dimension of 19, which is projected to the model dimension dd via a linear layer. Each output token encodes the validity indicator vtv_{t} and the final stone. The validity is one-hot encoded into a vector of dimension 2, and is concatenated with the final stone’s one-hot into a 15-dimensional vector, which is projected to dd via a separate linear layer.

For a trajectory of TT steps, the input sequence is constructed by interleaving input and output embeddings. For each timestep tt, the input embedding and output embedding are placed at positions 2​t2t and 2​t+12t+1, resulting in a sequence of length 2​T2T. The sequence is processed by a causal Transformer decoder with model dimension d=512d=512, MLP hidden dimension F=1024F=1024, N=12N=12 layers, H=8H=8 attention heads with head dimension d/H=64d/H=64.

Similar to Mastermind’s policy, the output prediction uses a GRU-based autoregressive decoder that conditions each output component’s prediction on the previously observed ground-truth components (teacher forcing during training). The per-step loss is the sum of the per-component negative log-probabilities: −∑k=15logp(ot(k)∣ot(1:k−1),ht)-\sum_{k=1}^{5}\log p(o_{t}^{(k)}\mid o_{t}^{(1:k-1)},h_{t}). The in-context world model is trained to minimize the cross-entropy loss of predicting the output at each step. In each training step, a fresh batch of B=64B=64 random trajectories is generated on-the-fly (no fixed dataset), and the model is optimized using Adam with a learning rate of 10−410^{-4}.

E.4.3 Policy

The policy is trained using PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization). At each training step, a batch of B=32B=32 trajectories of length T=5T=5 is collected by rolling out the current policy in the environment. The PPO objective uses K=4K=4 update epochs per batch of collected data.

Model Architecture

The policy is the same sequence model as used in Mastermind, with a Griffin backbone model (De et al., 2024), and a GRU to predict the final output components autoregressively conditioned on the Griffin’s output. The log-probability of the full action is the sum of the per-component log-probabilities: logπ(at∣st)=∑k=15logπk(at(k)∣st,at(1:k−1))\log\pi(a_{t}\mid s_{t})=\sum_{k=1}^{5}\log\pi_{k}(a_{t}^{(k)}\mid s_{t},a_{t}^{(1:k-1)}).
